#3717. Anthony Boyle Talks Sam Bankman-Fried and ‘The Altruists,’ a Tale of Sex and Crypto

Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the world, and who forged a charmingly slackerish persona: a shabbily dressed nerd with good intentions. As a believer in the effective altruism movement, SBF planned to donate his riches to charity. Instead, he is now serving a 25-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy.

Anthony Boyle slips under SBF’s skin in The Altruists, the new Netflix limited series chronicling the rise and fall of FTX—as well as the relationship between Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), his on-and-off romantic and business partner. The Belfast-born Boyle is best known to American audiences for his roles in historical dramas like House of Guinness (as 18th-century Irish lord Arthur Guinness), Say Nothing (as IRA leader Brendan Hughes), and Masters of the Air (as WW2 Air Force officer Harry Crosby). He got his break while still in college when he was cast as Scorpius Malfoy in the original cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child in London’s West End.

Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison, The Altruists, 2026.

Ellison’s character would love that. The geek love she and SBF share in the series is complicated and cringe-inducing. She writes Harry Potter fanfic and considers herself polyamorous; he’s a virgin wowed by her brainy sophistication. They egg each other on, bound together by their hunger for risk and their desire to win, whatever the game and whatever the cost. Throughout it all, they remain convinced that they are the good guys.

The Altruists drops November 19, in the midst of a Hollywood tech billionaire reckoning that includes the Sam Altman biopic Artificial, Musk, the Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything, and Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network, The Social Reckoning. Boyle says he hasn’t seen any of those films yet, though he was originally set to play SBF in another movie that fell through. “I was sort of heartbroken,” he tells me, “because I’d spent a couple of months prepping, I had turned down other projects, and then it was taken away from me. I was like, I’m never gonna be able to do that voice that I worked so hard on!”

Yet when his agent called with news of the Netflix project, Boyle was hesitant. “My heart was already broken by [SBF] once,” he says. But the scripts for The Altruist—written by Graham Moore, the screenwriter of The Imitation Game—changed his mind. “It’s so funny and more about the relationship between him and Caroline,” the actor says now, “about their love story and them goading each other to do all this.”

During his initial meeting with Moore, Boyle stayed in character as Bankman-Fried. “I

was complaining about getting off of a Zoom with Mark Zuckerberg, because that’s the tone of the show. It can be quite irreverent at some points, and then other scenes are kind of heartbreaking.” It won him the part. “Thankfully,” he says, “all my prep didn’t go to waste!”

Vanity Fair: It’s funny that you were so eager to live in Sam Bankman-Fried’s head. He is such an anxious figure.

Boyle: There’s a lot of anxiety in him. You can even tell in his speech patterns: He corrects himself and goes back and forth, like his internal metronome is going so quickly at all times. He’s like a hummingbird, like his heart’s beating so quick. But thankfully I didn’t take any of that home with me.

Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried, The Altruists, 2026.

At a couple of points in the series, he says, “I know I’m not a normal person.” There’s an ongoing public conversation right now about a lot of these tech moguls believing they know better than the rest of us. Did you think of SBF as someone with that kind of Superman complex?

I think the opposite. I played him as someone who was profoundly insecure. There’s this thing of broken men building empires. He has this idea of: I am FTX. So if I can make FTX the biggest, the richest, if I can have the most of something…. That’s not someone who’s comfortable in his own skin. I was interested in what possessed someone to become the world’s youngest billionaire. I’m not really interested in money or crypto or finance. It was: What makes them do the things that they do?

Sam is a nerdy guy, but as soon as he gets successful, he hangs giant posters of himself everywhere. Is he burning for the world to recognize him and admire his empire?

Do you know the poem “Ozymandias” [by Percy Bysshe Shelley]? There’s a bit in the show where I’m looking up at this great poster of myself, and it reminded me of that line: “Look on my works, ye mighty, and despair!” I asked Graham, “Can I quote that poem in the show?” And he said, “Originally called that episode ‘Ozymandias!’”

Talking about wanting to be recognized—when I was prepping for this, I went to a crypto guy’s birthday party in Los Angeles. He was paying a DJ a million dollars for one evening, but he built this plinth above the DJ decks for him and his friends so you had to look at him. A lot of these crypto people, who maybe didn’t have buzzing social lives—wallflowers who didn’t know how to communicate—became billionaires. And what this guy had done with it was to throw money at a very famous DJ, and then raise himself above him. It reminded me of the scene where Sam has a 100-foot poster behind him. It was like, Wow, this is that sort of man in his mum’s basement who just wants the world to see him.

In Sam’s case, his roaring egotism is somewhat awkward because he’s also obsessed with the idea of being altruistic. At one point in the show, a leader of the Effective Altruism movement sees this lavish party he’s thrown and says, “Uh, this isn’t very altruistic.”

Yes, he’s spent a lot of money on confetti cannons! That dichotomy is what’s really fascinating about him, because I think both of those two things are true. I think he really is altruistic, and I think he does have narcissistic tendencies.

I read that you corresponded with him in prison. What did you want to know?

Annoyingly for this interview, I promised him that I wouldn’t divulge anything. I asked him to open his heart up to me, and he really did. He was very forthcoming with over 100 questions in emails. He answered, I’d say, 98% of them. Even the ones that he didn’t answer were very telling for me, because you’re like a detective, trying to figure out how he answers them and in what way. And can you trust it?

As we see in the series, he insisted on doing interviews throughout the scandal. Even when his lawyers were telling him to stop.

When I was playing those scenes, it was like: I can outsmart this; I can get in front of it. I can just explain this to them. You know, he went to jail for stealing the money—but if he didn’t go to jail, a year later to the day, all of that money would have been back, and tenfold. He invested in Anthropic. He invested in the biggest AI companies. His argument was: Look, I know the markets. What you all see is a bird falling to certain death. What I can see is that the bird is swooping, and will come back up. I read last week that said Sam might have been the world’s first trillionaire had he not gone to jail, because all the AI companies are now flourishing.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried, The Altruists, 2026.

The show frames Sam and Caroline as a love story. But it’s hard to tell if they are egging on each other’s delusions, or if this is kind of a game that’s fueling their relationship.

They’re obsessed with games. Even the first time they meet, they are playing a game. This isn’t in the show, but in my head, the scene that I sort of created for myself to understand him was: He’s playing World of Warcraft, and on the same screen he loses $100 million, and then he dies in World of Warcraft. He’s like, Fuck!, and feels more emotional about the game than about other people’s money.

It does feel like the real-life consequences are very abstract to him. Like he’s busy trying to outplay everyone and not thinking: This is going to cause somebody to go bankrupt and ruin their lives.

I think that’s the great tragedy of it, because people did go bankrupt, and people unfortunately died by suicide through this. Marriages broke up. Families tore apart because all of their money was in this. And that’s something that we have to remember when talking about the show. There were real-world consequences because of this crash.

There’s a whole spate of movie projects this fall that suggest tech bros are the new supervillains. But it sounds like you didn’t approach the character that way at all.

My viewpoint on it is that Sam wants to do good. But I think the best-laid plans of mice and men often [go awry]. It’s easy to say I’m going to give away all these billions—and then suddenly you’re not in your mum’s basement, and you’re hanging out with Katy Perry, and you think, This feels pretty good to me. I don’t think people should have that amount of power.

You are Mr. Period Actor. Is this the first time that you’ve played a character living in the present?

I feel like it is. It’s the first time I had to act with a laptop and an iPhone, and it’s so annoying. There’s no one there that you’re looking at. You’re just looking at a green screen. And then it [causes problems]—like, Oh, we saw the camera in the reflection when you turned it that way. These things that I didn’t have to deal with before because I was, as you said, Mr. Period Man.

Even Say Nothing was set in the 1970s and ’80s, well before cell phones.

One of your most recent period characters is Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness, and there’s been some buzz about your full-frontal nude scene on that show. I’m just curious if there’s anything that you would not do on screen.

That’s such a funny question. I guess whatever they write in the script, I’d look at it and see if I wanted to do it, but probably not! Like when I did that scene, it was in service of the character and in service of the moment. I wanted that character to feel like he's in control of the world and that these are all peasants that are beneath him and he doesn’t care. Very opposite to Sam, who I think has a lot of body shame.

Somehow, I don’t know that the world wants to think about Sam Bankman-Fried naked.

You never know, man. There’s something out there for everyone.

#3716. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.

Preorders are opening up for physical editions of Nightdive's Thief Remaster, and at the high end, the studio is offering an homage to Thief's iconic original PC big box packaging in that shape we all know and love, the trapezoid. The only problem? Nightdive and partner Clear River Games are only offering it for Switch/Switch 2 and PS5.

It doesn't really, at least not as much as war and death and politics or whatever. But Thief's original '90s big box edition came in a jaunty little trapezoidal box unlike anything else on the market. It remains a visually striking, highly sought-after collector's item. It's fun, it's memorable, and it's a piece of PC gaming history. I've had to settle for my version of Thief Gold that came in a plain Jane regular box as a reissue.

It's not super surprising that Night Dive and Clear River eschewed a PC version of this physical release⁠—that's fairly common these days, even in boutique indie special editions. I had a similar "we're so back, it's so over" reaction when I saw that indie RPG heater Dread Delusion's limited physical edition had skipped PC.

But the hurt feels new all over again when it's a PC gaming icon like Thief, and a PC gaming phenomenon like the big box. I would have dropped a fat hundo on a physical PC version of Thief Remastered in a heartbeat⁠—it's why I live in an apartment and not a house.

And studios still do come out with physical editions of their PC games: My Baldur's Gate 3 big box has pride of place in my office. All told, it's just a slight bummer and frustration trying to drag down one of my most anticipated games. I'm still going to play the hell out of it when it comes out on December 3, though.

I'm rooting for GOG's proposal to bring back the big box. The company seems to be considering a boutique service where you can purchase physical versions of the games in your library, which sounds pretty rad to me.

#3714. Google’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Egg Makes The Search Engine What It Always Should’ve Been

GoogleThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Google’s cashing in on the nostalgia reawakened by the Ocarina of Time remake. If you type “zelda” into the Google search bar, you’ll get a glowing, hovering Master Sword in the bottom right-hand corner of the screen. Click it, and the browser transports you and the search engine back in time to 1998, when everything was good and nothing hurt, or at least when it wasn’t an absolute pain in the ass to try to find something via Google.

The Google page is bedecked in its old livery: the bygone logo with the exclamation mark, along with old blue links in Times New Roman-ish font and listed, blessedly, in order of importance and relevance. No AI search results, no pesky shopping links, no ads. It’s a big ol’ beacon reminding you of a time when the web held the promise of unlimited information at your fingertips, and wasn’t yet the enshittified, barely ethical infomercial it has become. All for a little “Zelda” joke.

It’s not just “zelda” that’ll get you the nostalgia easter egg. “Ocarina of Time” will get you there too. It’s actually quite funny that Google’s reminding us now of the time when it didn’t suck. Last week, Google lost $475 billion in stock market value, the company’s worst-performing day on the stock market ever, with analysts noting that it had missed its ad revenue targets. The reason: Its own AI search product was eating into that ad revenue. Maybe Google should make the Zelda easter egg last a little longer.

When it comes to the list of upcoming Marvel shows, fans are set to witness the end of an era in 2027. Daredevil: Born Again is set to end next year following a three-season run. Fans have, unsurprisingly, been in their feelings since the news was confirmed, and the cast has been opening up as well. Franchise veteran Deborah Ann Woll also spoke out in the aftermath of the cancellation news. And, more recently, she got real about one way this series’ demise differs from that of its parent show.

Woll has not only played Karen on Born Again, but she famously portrayed the journalist-turned-lawyer on Netflix’s Daredevil as well. Given that personal history, Woll has become quite attached to her character and this corner of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The fan-favorite actress recently spoke to ComicBook about her time with the franchise and reflected on the first show’s cancellation. Per Woll, the third season of that show is her favorite of the series, and that was just one reason why the cancellation initial stung:

I mean, I think the first time we were canceled, we really didn’t know it was coming, right? Like, that third season of the Netflix one is my favorite of the three. And I thought it was really a high point in the series, and we fully expected to come back and do more. So I didn’t really get to say goodbye, and that felt like the rug being pulled out from under us.

Woll’s feelings are completely understandable, as Daredevil’s cancellation in 2018 was heartbreaking. At the time, the show’s unfortunate fate was in great part due to the shrinking role of the now-defunct Marvel Television (a banner now used by Marvel Studios’ TV arm). It’s sad to think about the notion of the True Blood alum both being surprised by the show’s conclusion and being unable to properly say goodbye to her colleagues. At the very least, though, with Born Again’s cancellation, Woll was afforded more closure:

This one? You know, you’re never sure, but I think we all sort of felt like this was the last one… as we were wrapping things up. And so, you know, I stole something from the set, and I hugged everybody I wanted to hug. And I will say this: having played a character over twelve years, you get to see someone go through such different stages of their life. And I really appreciated that they let the story take that change.

While I’m comforted by the notion of Woll having had an inkling regarding Born Again’s fate, it’s still hard to believe the show is coming to an end. There’s been quite a bit of mourning amongst fans in some respects, but the stars themselves are remaining upbeat. Series lead Charlie Cox shared a great perspective, as he emphasized how he and his collaborators are going out on their own terms. Fellow cast member Matthew Lillard also teased an exciting third season, and those comments may cheer up fans.

It’s true that there will be a lot to look forward to in this third and final season, from a loose adaptation of the famous storyline “"The Devil in Cell-Block D" to a reunion of The Defenders. Of course, we’ll also get to spend more time with Deborah Ann Woll’s Karen Page, who’s proven to be one of the MCU’s most dynamic characters. It’ll be a pleasure for me to watch her in the final season, and it’ll be sweeter knowing that Page was able to walk away from set after having given hugs and snagged a souvenir.

Daredevil: Born Again Season 3 is set to premiere in March 2027 and, in the meantime, fans can stream the first two seasons (along with the OG show) using a Disney+ subscription.

#3712. I Tested ChatGPT's New 'Slides' Tool, and Here's How It Compares to Gemini

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

ChatGPT's capabilities continue to expand apace, and the latest feature is a fully capable slideshow creator. Announced a few weeks ago, ChatGPT Slides lets you create PowerPoint-style decks from inside your conversations, and it's now appearing for those on the Pro tier and above (meaning right now, you need to spend at least $100 a month to get it).

If you're on the free ChatGPT plan or the $20-a-month Plus tier, you can still get ChatGPT to generate downloadable PowerPoint files from the content of your conversations. However, they'll be more basic than those made in the full version of ChatGPT Slides, and there are no collaboration or native edit options.

ChatGPT Slides is part of OpenAI's push to give users a complete office suite inside the ChatGPT apps. Pages (the word processor) is already available for Pro tiers and above, while a spreadsheet app is on the way—the idea being that you will soon be able to get all your work done without any help from Google or Microsoft.

While Chatgpt Slides is only available on pricey plans right now, it's likely to come to lower subscription tiers in the future. But for now, how does the tool compare to what's available in the free and Plus tiers, not to mention what you can do with Gemini inside Google Slides? I've taken a detailed look.

When it comes to testing out AI tools, it helps to focus on something you're already knowledgeable about so you can spot any mistakes. To test this, I decided to see what ChatGPT could hoover up from the web about the new iPhone Duo. If you're on the free or Plus plans, you can start a conversation, then ask for a slideshow or PowerPoint about it.

Plus accounts also have access to a specific Presentations add-on, available via the + (plus) menu in the prompt box, though I get the impression this feature is in a state of flux since ChatGPT Slides arrived. In any case, you can begin asking about the iPhone Duo specs and early online reactions, and then say "build me a slideshow on the key features and reviews so far".

What I got back on the $20 Plus account was a fairly competent slideshow on Apple's foldable, with accurate information as far as I could see, and a simple series of layouts. It looked like something you might whip up from a template if you were in a rush and didn't have time to properly align all the bullet points or be very selective about which details you included and which you left out. One neat touch is that ChatGPT was able to drop in an official photo of the iPhone Duo at the start of the slideshow, but I had to specifically ask for one.

You can go back and make specific edits to the slideshow, but you have to describe them in the general prompt box—you can't select individual slide elements and make more precise changes. Still, if all you want to do is occasionally convert your ChatGPT conversations into a rough and ready slideshow, there's no real need to upgrade from the free or Plus accounts for now.

Switching to a Pro account, I gave a similar task to ChatGPT Slides hoping for something more comprehensive. To begin with, Slides gets its own dedicated area in the app, so you can start up a blank presentation from scratch—there are some basic image and text features, but the idea is to use prompts to build your slide deck. It's like a really basic Google Slides, with a prompt box.

Creating a slideshow this way feels rather tedious: Typing out what you want to say and then waiting for ChatGPT to do it isn't as intuitive as just throwing in some graphics and text yourself, as you might do in PowerPoint. It also seems to be a bit buggy, at least during the time I spent testing it, with some requests not properly completing.

Starting a standard conversation with ChatGPT and then turning all the information into a deck is much more useful from my perspective. My iPhone Duo slideshow was longer, laid out better, and more informative than the one I created on the Plus plan—there were even charts of battery life and official photos this time.

However, whether I used the free, Plus, or Pro tools, my presentations didn't come across as particularly well thought through. They don't really flow smoothly, either across individual slides or the slideshow as a whole—it feels very much like an algorithm, rather than a person, has decided what information to include and where on the slides to stick it.

Whether you create presentations in chats or through the ChatGPT Slides space, you're able to click on individual elements and do some basic manual resizing and repositioning. You can also request edits via prompts: "Drop in an image of a cat", "make this pop more", "center all of this information", or whatever it is.

ChatGPT Slides does offer collaborative tools, which I wasn't able to test, and I can see that being useful for teams heavily invested in ChatGPT's ecosystem. I can also imagine ChatGPT Slides coming in handy when you've got a lot of information you need to quickly dump into a slideshow that looks vaguely presentable.

In general though, I think I'd much rather stick to the traditional way of making slideshows for now. These old methods are more precise and more manageable, and give you full control over what's shown and where—even if they do take a bit longer. What's more, modern-day presentation tools come with so many templates and other layout aids that it's not difficult to put together something that's easy on the eyes while including all of the information you think is most critical.

Google is, of course, also all the way in on AI (and then some), and if you pay for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or above, you can have Gemini pop up right inside Google Slides to give you some assistance with your presentation-making. To compare the tools, I gave it the same task as I did ChatGPT, asking for a slide deck on the new iPhone Duo.

Gemini actually asked some questions along the way: about wht visual style to use, the audience to aim the slideshow at, and the details to highlight. Though it's always possible to put this sort of information manually into a prompt, this would be a helpful additional to ChatGPT Slides.

What Gemini and Google Slides produced was impressive in terms of the layout and overall vibe of the presentation: It felt much more like a human being had put together the slide deck compared to what ChatGPT had produced, in terms of the information chosen, the way the slides were laid out, and the color picks.

However, Google's result had its faults too: The presentation got the facts on the maximum brightness of the iPhone Duo screen wrong, and produced an "iPhone Duo" graphic that looked like two iPhones from around 2021 stuck together. ChatGPT Slides at least managed to pull official imagery from the Apple website.

You can't attach individual edit prompts to specific parts of your presentation in Google Slides as you can in ChatGPT Slides—you have to mention them in the general prompt box. That said, Google Slides is obviously a much more mature and established slideshow tool compared to the OpenAI equivalent, in terms of its features and layout options (it has been around for a decade, after all).

Given that extra software structure and the lower cost of entry, Gemini and Google Slides is the better option for AI-assisted slideshow making at the moment—though I wouldn't bet against OpenAI catching up. For now, ChatGPT Slides is something that's good to have available if you're already paying a lot for ChatGPT every month, but not a feature that makes it worth your while to swap your AI allegiance.

U.S. President Donald Trump recently hosted several celebrities at the White House for dinner, with one of those guests being Bill Maher. Sometime later, POTUS took to social media and chastised Maher, who has joked about Trump on air on multiple ocassions. In the aftermath, Maher addressed the situation on the latest episode of his talk show (which is streamable with an HBO Max subscription). With that, the comedian dropped a joke relating to Kelly Clarkson.

Last weekend, President Trump shared his thoughts on Maher (and more topics) to Truth Social, and the post ended up including a total of 1,318 words. In the lengthy post, Trump refers to Maher as a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” with “a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO” and capitalized those specific words as well. The President’s post came days after remarks Maher shared on Real Time days prior. The comic joked about Trump’s supposed focus on “men’s bodies” and mused that he himself was not complimented during dinner.

Amid the latest installment of Real Time – which aired on October 30th amid the 2026 TV schedule – Maher touched on several topics before shifting his focus to Trump’s viral post. The political humorist didn’t mince words when describing the aftermath of the post, and he not only name-dropped Clarkson but a certain pop star as well:

He went off on me like Kelly Clarkson in a toy store. I mean, eating with Trump is like dating Taylor Swift. It’s a lot of laughs at the time, but later on, they’re tearing you a new asshole.

The Major CBS News Claims Bari Weiss Apparently Shared With Bill Maher: ‘I Was Curious’

Bill Maher’s Taylor Swift comment seemingly references how the singer’s exes remain topics of discussion on social media even after they’ve dated. The Clarkson sentiment, however, refers to a situation that’s a bit more recent. Back in October, Clarkson posted about a negative experience she reportedly had at Art of Play, a novelty store located in Brooklyn. The singer claimed she was treated like Julia Roberts’ character from Pretty Woman when she attempted to buy a singing bird automaton.

However, the store’s management team – headed up by owner Adam Rubin – later claimed the bird was not for sale and was used for in-store events. However, Clarkson later responded to the claim by sharing a photo of the bird with a $15,000 price tag on it. Leaked security footage later revealed that Clarkson had a heated exchange with store employees. As it stands, Rubin and co. have been receiving hate on social media and have reportedly been seeking to reach out to Clarkson.

As of this writing, Kelly Clarkson has reportedly yet to touch base with the crew at Art of Play. On that note, Donald Trump has yet to respond to Maher’s latest comments regarding his post and their dinner at the White House. Whether he’ll choose to do so remains to be seen.

#3709. This New Garmin Feature Is Draining Battery Life, but There's a Quick Fix

Garmin users are taking to the company's support forums with a common grievance: The newly introduced "OK Garmin" hands-free voice feature appears to be eating through battery life. The feature arrived through Garmin’s September software updates, bringing hands-free voice activation to the Fenix 8, Forerunner 570 and 970, Venu 4, and several other models. Here's how to make sure Garmin's new updates aren't slashing your watch's battery life.

Last month's updates for select watches also brought all-day fall detection, a set of new Quick Workouts and Garmin Run Coach plans, as well as that "OK Garmin" hands-free voice command feature. It's exactly what it sounds like: Instead of pressing a button, users can simply say “OK Garmin” to activate voice commands. However, it looks like "OK Garmin" in particular is what causes some watch's projected runtimes to drastically drop, allegedly by roughly 35% to 50% in some cases.

Garmin does acknowledge that enabling these settings shortens battery life, though it doesn't say by how much. The tradeoff makes sense, since the watch has to listen constantly for its wake phrase. Even so, giving up several days of runtime is a steep price for a feature that many people may seldom use. Luckily, the fix is simple: Turning off "OK Garmin" should restore your battery life estimates right away.

If your watch has been draining faster since the update, go to Settings > System > Voice and disable "OK Garmin." If needed, you can also switch off the Phone Assistant wake word from the same area. The good news is that turning this feature off won't even take voice commands away—you can still trigger them manually using the watch's physical controls.

Keep in mind that these numbers are battery estimates rather than independently tested, real-world runtimes. Some of the battery complaints that surfaced after the update may also stem from unrelated issues. Still, trading away as much as half your battery life just to avoid pressing a button is a difficult bargain to defend.

With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

I must admit, I was mighty intrigued by the idea of a modern mouse (and all their high DPI machinations) with a screen slapped on the side, but I must also admit I thought we would be over the growing pains by now, what with screens being slammed into everything from cases to coolers to controllers.

Yet one look at the Turtle Beach Command Series MC7 suggests those growing pains are still being suffered. And using the mouse only confirms it.

But I get the idea in concept. I'm a big fan of my Stream Deck, and find myself regularly using its many controls. Being able to shove those into the side of the mouse with clarity to read what they're doing is intriguing. It's also particularly effective when it comes to swapping DPI, polling rate, and even checking the battery. Those are things that do benefit from a visual component. And yet a few weeks with the MC7 have convinced me I won't be making the swap full time.

✅ You gotta have a large screen on your mouse: As far as I can see, this is the only gaming mouse with modern specs and a big screen from a reputable brand out there.

❌ You want a mouse for competitive gaming: The MC7 is simply not comfortable nor snappy enough for competitive gaming❌ You don't need a large screen on your mouse: We've seen small OLED screens from the likes of SteelSeries and CoolerMaster if you're simply looking for something to display figures.

With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

Wired and wireless (2.4 GHz and Bluetooth)

Internally, the MC7 has impressive stats. Its Owl-Eye Optical sensor goes all the way up to a max DPI of 30,000, and the polling rate of 8,000 Hz is competitive-level. That's so high, in fact, that the average person won't even see the benefit of it.

And the elephant in the room here: the 2.25-inch colour display is touch-sensitive too, which means you can flick through a couple of different screens depending on your use case. We have seen screens on gaming mice before, like the Cooler Master MM830 and SteelSeries Rival 710 (neither of which are touch screens), but as far as I can tell, the MC7 is the largest on a modern gaming mouse from a reputable brand. That makes it an oddity at the least.

But that's not all the MC7 has going for it. The 4D scroll wheel means you can go up, down, left and right on a page with just the wheel, and you have extra buttons here, too. You have one at the bottom of the thumb rest, another next to the mouse wheel, plus two on the left-hand side, as well as your standard clicks.

It's a wireless mouse, so it comes with a 2.4 GHz receiver, and it also has hot-swappable batteries. The battery charger has a spare USB Type-A port, which means your charger can also be the receiver. This is a sweet system, which makes the MC7 feel like it has infinite battery (as long as you are willing to spend twenty seconds swapping the battery every 10 or so hours).

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The Owl-Eye sensor is great. It's consistent and smooth, and never posed any problems in any of the games I threw this mouse at. For everyday gaming, I don't have any complaints about how its internals performed. It's a slightly customised version of the PixArt PAW3950 sensor, and will be familiar to anyone who's used the Razer Deathadder V3 Pro, which previously had the exclusive use of PixArt's 30K sensor.

The mouse clicks are a tad loud for my liking, but they're plenty snappy. This bad boy is fitted with Titan Optical switches, and they are perfect under my fingertips. I have yet to hit a single double-click and find them to be very responsive.

However, the biggest problem with performance is how the MC7's weight is balanced and how it feels under the palms. At 135 g grams, it's a fairly heavy mouse (more so than the recent Naga V3 Pro and its mountain of buttons), but this wouldn't be too big of a problem if it could balance that weight in a comfortable way.

However, it feels clunky, and even has a slight rattle at high speeds. This all contributes to a mouse that feels a little lacking in competitive play, even though it's got the internal chops to handle everything on paper.

In use, the screen is rather peculiar. Via the Turtle Beach Swarm II software, you can flit between a few screens, which you customise with your own controls, and they are fairly snappy and responsive. However, having to arch my fingers to actually click on the screen means it's not intended for quick play. That makes it better as a micro function, or a way of displaying battery (but the device's lighting can already indicate battery life and DPI setting). It can display things like health and ammo in Counter-Strike 2, but its viewing angles are pretty poor, meaning it doesn't offer much of a tactical advantage.

The MC7 comes with two 1000 mAh batteries, both of which are hot-swappable. They connect to a charger (which also has a USB port for your 2.4 GHz connector), and this means you technically only need one USB to do everything for your mouse. It's a great system.

To swap the batteries out, you simply take off a compartment where your palm rests, pull the battery out and put a new one in. The MC7's onboard battery is just big enough that I've never noticed the device dying while I'm changing batteries. It's pretty sweet, and with a little practice, it can be swapped in seconds. It's not quite as quick to swap as the Glorious Model O Eternal, with its open battery system, but it is a bit tidier.

Working on my PC every day, then gaming most nights, I found myself swapping out the battery every few days at 1,000 Hz polling, which is perfectly solid given how convenient swapping the batteries is.

The MC7 is a very confusing mouse in regard to its ergonomics. The groove on the left-hand side for your thumb is comfortable and intuitive, yet the two buttons on either side of that groove are awkward to get to. My left thumb buttons on a mouse tend to be going forward and backwards on a page, and therefore I like to have instant access to them. I don't have that access here, and have to physically bend my thumb or extend it to get to each button. The groove also has a texture to it, which is clearly designed so the mouse doesn't slip, and that's also quite strange, as it feels like you aren't encouraged to move your thumb, and yet you have to in order to hit those two buttons.

The back of the mouse curves to my palm well, but the two mouse click buttons are quite curved in the centre. That means, if I hold my hand on the bottom of the mouse, there's air underneath the bottom of my fingers as I hold it, and if I put my palm forward, then there's air underneath my knuckles. I feel like, no matter what way I hold the mouse, I'm holding it just a little wrong.

That's before getting to the screen, a panel that is too long to use all of it while on the go, and close enough to my fingers that I constantly change my DPI whenever I take my hand off the mouse and put it back on again. Perhaps the strangest element of this is that I couldn't seem to figure out a way to lock the screen, which would really make it much better for gaming.

For quickly changing a song or pausing a video, I actually found myself taking my left finger off the left click and wrapping it around the display instead. As far as I can tell, there just isn't a quick and comfortable way to get to all parts of the screen with ease, and I have quite large hands too.

As far as build quality is concerned, the MC7 doesn't feel cheap under the palm, though I'm not a fan of the vibration you get when you click the screen. It just has a hollow feel and sound. The texture on the mouse is cool to the fingertips, and it handles fingerprints well. Despite the fact that you have to take the back cover off to pop the batteries in, I could never get it to come off accidentally either, which is always a plus.

There is a slight rattle if you pick up the mouse and shake it, and that rattle appears to be coming from the 4D mouse wheel. Generally, you don't tend to shake mice, but if you pick it up quickly to move it from one side of the mousepad to the other, it does produce the rattling sound.

One thing I do quite like is a button sunken into the left thumbgrip. I can hold that down and move the rather great-feeling scroll wheel to change volume in an instant, and this is handier and quicker than using the touch screen's volume icons.

The MC7 is clearly intended to fit in alongside the likes of the Turtle Beach Stealth Pro II with its combination of copper and black, but it doesn't have the sleekness of its headset counterpart. Instead, it's more Cronenbergian, a collection of skewed angles and bumps, like the tech parts inside its shell are clamouring to get out and your hand is the thing holding them in. It's almost like two separate gaming mice have accidentally stepped inside the teleporter and what has come out is a wretched combination of both.

The right-hand side is relatively low to the ground and with little detailing, whereas the left side is angular, sharp and tall. This is naturally so tall because there's a screen slapped on the side, but it means the entire mouse has a slant going to the right.

Despite this slant, the front is cut at quite a sharp angle too. The MC7 is kind of curvy, and kind of not. It's kind of angular, and also kind of not. It's a hard shape to make sense of and, to my eyes, pretty darn ugly on top of my desk.

One element I do like about the MC7's aesthetic is its choice of RGB. You get a sleek line of it just underneath the mouse, which is customizable, but it glows red when the battery is low, which is a good reminder when I've needed it. The screen also alerts you when your battery is low.

As far as the display is concerned, it has colour, which is a nice touch, but also has weirdly poor viewing angles. If I look at the screen from the position I'd usually game from, it can look washed out. It never looks so washed out that I can't roughly guess what its icons are (and with time, you learn their position anyway), but it makes it feel less quality than the black and copper might suggest.

For the first few weeks with this mouse, I found Turtle Beach's Swarm II to be a mostly fine bit of software, though it could be a little slow. However, this week, the latest update, Software version 1.0.0.63 (which launched on November 2), has seemingly entirely broken on my PC. I can't get it to open, though it remains open in Task Manager. Given it only just launched, I could see this issue being fixed quickly, but it's a shame that so much software for hardware is not consistent.

It is also a necessary bit of software if you would like to customise the screen. With it downloaded, the screen is customizable much like a Stream Deck. Grab widgets from within the app, the mouse's onboard memory, or third-party apps, slap them on the screen, and now you have a new shortcut. Without it, there's not much you can do.

And, as far as I can tell, you can't set totally custom controls, as you can do with the Stream Deck, which limits your customisation a tad. But it's still pretty broad for the most part, and I've rarely found myself looking for a shortcut and not been able to find it.

$160 is a lot of cash for a gaming mouse. It's so much money, in fact, that you can pick up the best gaming mouse out there, the Razer Viper V4 Pro, with its impeccable sensor, great battery life, and lightweight feel, for the same price.

As such, you can pick an overall better, lighter mouse for the same price, or go for the screen. The battery system is certainly neat, though there are other mice out there with hot-swappable batteries.

The MC7 doesn't detract from day-to-day gaming, but I'd much prefer a lower base polling rate if it meant a cheaper price point, as this isn't exactly a competitive-level mouse in function.

It is clear where the budget for this build goes. A large screen couldn't be cheap; the material feels good on the fingertips, and that's before mentioning the research and development costs associated with getting a touchscreen on a mouse. However, it's so much money that, to my palms, it only really feels like the first step for Turtle Beach. It's like a test run of what a touchscreen could be like, and for this price, I don't quite see the vision.

3. Best budget wireless: Mchose G3 V2 Pro

4. Best budget wired: Glorious Model O Eternal

5. Best competitive:Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike

6. Best lightweight: Corsair Sabre V2 Pro

7. Best MMO: Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE

With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

#3706. Oscar Chances for Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 'You Can See Everything’

The biggest star of Oscar season may be a woman who can’t even attend.

This past month, one name has been circling around Hollywood more than any other: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. The documentary You Can See Everything— which follows Holmes during the 34 days leading up to her 11-year prison sentence for fraud (now reduced to 10 years)—has become a must-see sensation and a box-office hit. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the three-hour film starts out as an intimate portrait of Holmes as she spends her days with her husband Billy Evans and their two children, and then transforms into a much wilder investigation as Fielder tries to make sense of Holmes and Evans’s relationship and intentions.

[Editor’s Note: Spoilers from You Can See Everything ahead.]

We’ve already covered the most shocking revelations from the A24 film, but another big twist could be coming: You Can See Everything is very likely to become the first documentary ever nominated for best picture.

For most of Oscar history, documentaries have been sequestered to the best documentary category. In 98 years, a doc has never been nominated for best picture, even after the category expanded from 5 to 10 nominees in 2010.

The film that got closest to a best-picture nomination was the 1994 documentary Hoop Dreams. Critic Roger Ebert had deemed the documentary the best movie of the year and pushed for its inclusion in the best picture lineup. But not only did Hoop Dreams miss that category, it didn’t even get nominated for best documentary. This led to an outcry, and in his 1995 essay “Anatomy of a Snub,” Ebert took stock of the five documentary nominees and decreed Hoop Dreams better than all of them. “What is obvious is that the committee that chose this year’s Oscar nominees were fond of documentaries about things that have already happened. They do not seem receptive to cinema verite,” he wrote.

The uproar over Hoop Dreams’s omission led to major changes in how the documentary nominees were voted on, and was also the starting point for the creation of a documentary branch within the Academy, which was established in 2001.

The genre has come a long way since then, with several films becoming major moments within the zeitgeist, like 2002’s Bowling for Columbine, 2006’s An Inconvenient Truth (which won for documentary feature and original song), and more recently, films like Free Solo and My Octopus Teacher.

Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything.

You Can See Everything’s toughest race may be in the documentary category itself. The documentary branch, which selects the nominees, has gained a reputation for snubbing popular documentaries, including the Mr. Rogers film Won’t You Be My Neighbor? (2018) and the Jon Batiste doc American Symphony (2023).

Celebrity-centered docs have had an especially hard time gaining recognition, including Will Ferrell’s Will & Harper, I Am: Celine Dion, Elton John: Never Too Late, Super/Man: The Christopher Reeve Story, and Mariska Hargitay’s My Mom Jayne.

Will this branch view You Can See Everything as too popular or too celebrity-centered, with Fielder, who is known for starring in his TV series The Rehearsal and Nathan for You, as not only one of the filmmakers but also a participant in the film? The shortlists, which come out on December 15, will be the film’s first test in the doc category.

You Can See Everything could also make history if it’s nominated in more than three categories. It’s still rare for a documentary to get nominated outside of the doc category, but editing, cinematography, and directing feel like possible nods for the film. Only two docs have even been nominated in three categories before: At the 1971 Oscars, Woodstock won best documentary and was also nominated for editing and sound, and 2021’s Flee was nominated for best documentary feature, animated feature, and international feature.

And what about the possibility of Amanda Seyfried, who makes a surprise appearance in the film, landing a nomination for supporting actress? You Can See Everything blurs the lines between doc and narrative storytelling when Seyfried steps back into her The Dropout role, playing Holmes in Fielder’s reenactments of scenes that he was unable to film for the documentary. A source tells Vanity Fair that A24 is still deciding if she’ll be submitted for supporting actress, but some awards prognosticator sites already have her popping up as a potential nominee.

An individual in a documentary has never been nominated in an acting category because, of course, there aren’t usually actors playing other characters in a nonfiction film. The closest comparison from Oscar history would be Maria Bakalova, who landed a supporting actress nomination in 2021 for her performance in Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a mockumentary sequel in which she played a fictional character opposite real people like Rudy Giuliani and Mike Pence.

You Can See Everything will have challenges at other awards shows on its way to the Oscars. The Golden Globes’ rules currently state that only “feature-length, scripted motion pictures” are eligible for the drama and comedy motion picture categories and that “live-action or animated documentaries and docudramas with over 25% of documentary footage or audio are considered documentaries and, therefore, are not eligible for consideration as motion pictures.” The Actor Awards (formerly known as the SAG Awards) has also never included a documentary, and the rules explicitly state “documentaries are not eligible.”

The Directors Guild of America recently confirmed to Variety that Fielder and Oppenheim are only eligible to compete in the outstanding directorial achievement in documentary category and not in the group’s most high-profile prize, outstanding directorial achievement in theatrical feature film. Their rules state that “re-releases, animated films and documentaries are not eligible” for the theatrical feature film award, which has aligned with the winner of the best-director Oscar for the majority of its existence, including the past six years straight.

Any of these voting bodies could bend their rules for this genre-bending film, or they may not. We’re in uncharted waters here. But if a documentary finally cracks best picture after 98 years, it will be fitting that it’s one as unique as this—and that its main character won’t be walking the red carpet.

#3704. This Is the Robot Vacuum I Use Every Day, and It's 50% Off Right Now

I live in a 1,600-square-foot home, and vacuuming and mopping it by hand takes a considerable chunk of time. Passing that labor off to a robot vacuum was a great decision. I decided to go with the Roborock Qrevo CurvX since it seemed like a great fit for my circumstances. If you also have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, this robot vacuum might work for you, too. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been, according to price-tracking tools.

One of the main things I was looking for in a robot vacuum was suction power. The Qrevo CurvX has 22,000 Pa, which is stronger than most options at its price and is powerful enough to pick up anything that needs vacuuming in my house. I like that it has a self-lifting chassis so it can climb over my workout mat, rugs, obstacles like cables, or anything else that might be in the way, so I don't have to babysit it while it's doing its job. I also like the extendable mop pads and side brushes that allow it to reach corners and crevices it might not be slim enough to fit into. (Speaking of which, it's only 3.14 inches tall, so it can fit under most couches and beds without issue.)

My experience with the Roborock app has been great. It's easy to use and gives me enough control to clean my house how I want without a hassle. "No Go Zones" are easy to set up, as is the schedule. The main issue I've had is the size of the internal dust bin: It's small, so it needs to be cleaned after basically every scheduled use (though that shouldn't be as bad if you don't have a pet that sheds a lot).

Take it from me: If you're looking for a reliable hybrid robot vacuum that can clean multiple types of floors, mop, and comes with a great app, the Qrevo CurvX makes a compelling case at the current $750 discount.

#3703. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Devs Tried Adding Even More Fast Travel Points, But That Sucked

The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out this week, and by all accounts we’ve heard so far, it seems like a pretty faithful remake, albeit with a lot of (necessary, in my opinion) technical and mechanical smoothing out from the original. I don’t envy the devs working on this one (which we now know to be Nintendo EPD): Ocarina of Time is a classic that everyone has really, really strong feelings about. Deciding what to change and what not to change must have been a huge headache.

Which is why I’m so, so glad that Eiji Aonuma backtracked on his own ridiculous idea to add a bunch of new fast-travel pointsÂ to this game.

This came up during an Ask the Developer interview published by Nintendo today. Now, the original Ocarina of Time already has some fast travel, in that Link can eventually learn ocarina songs that will warp him to each of five of the game’s major dungeons, plus the Temple of Time. And honestly, that’s quite enough to be getting on with, thanks. One of these songs is actually necessary to even access its associated dungeon in the first place, as you need child Link at the Desert Colossus, but he can’t get into Gerudo Valley without being adult Link and riding Epona.

But at one point in the remake’s development, longtime Zelda producer and franchise steward Eiji Aonuma thought this wasn’t enough. As Aonuma explains, he observed that a lot of players tried to move around the world faster in the original by spamming Link’s dodge roll, which led him to think there may need to be a faster way to get around the world.

I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didnât exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, âWait, whatâs this?â Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren’t working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again. (Laughs)

Honestly, what a relief. He’s spot on, really. I played Ocarina of Time for the first time back in January, and while there were times when I was grateful to have a quick way to get from, say, Zora’s Domain all the way back to Castle Town without hoofing it through multiple loading zones I’ve seen a dozen times before, a lot of my favorite discoveries in this game came from being forced to hike around and trip over interesting things. There are all sorts of hidden bits in Hyruleâheart pieces, rupees, goofy little characters.

I also just don’t know where you’d even put more fast travel points. I guess I can imagine Aonuma wanting to add warp points to places like Kokiri Forest, Lon Lon Ranch, Zora’s Domain, and other major spots. But if you did that, then why would you ever need to even be in Hyrule Field? Ocarina of Time is not a massive game! It does not take that long to cross Hyrule Field, especially on Epona! It’s pretty easy to get to all those spots from the temple warps! Kids these days don’t want to go on long walks through grassy, Peahat-ridden plains anymore!

Mostly I just think it’s funny that Aonuma both proposed this idea and ultimately rejected it. Elsewhere in the interview, Aonuma talks about how the development of this remake involved handing off this old classic to individuals who had never played it until they were put on the project and letting them make their own decisions about how much to alter:

If the producers say, âThis is how it should be,â the team would naturally feel obligated to do it that way. So I basically let the developers make whatever changes they genuinely felt were necessary. I wanted the team to make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time their own, and to follow through on their own ideas about what the game should be. That said, I did deliver my fair share of lectures along the way. (Laughs) I took a step back to observe how the younger members of the development team would reimagine The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using the insights and answers they had arrived at on their own.

The remake of Ocarina of Time is out later this week, on November 5, and a second part of this Ask the Developer interview is dropping tomorrow. You should read the entirety of it when you get the chance, as it’s pretty neat, though it’s left me desperately wanting to hear whatever “bright and upbeat” piece of music Kondo originally composed for Ganondorf’s theme way back in the ’90s.

Nagoshi Studio revealed Gang of Dragon less than a year ago, but it ran into trouble just a few months later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Six months after the disappearance of Nagoshi Studio's website, a Google-translated notice in the Japan government's Kanpo website (via Gematsu) says the company has now officially closed its doors.

Founded by Yakuza creator Toshihiro Nagoshi in 2021 after a run of more than 30 years at Sega, Nagoshi Studio's first game was revealed at the 2025 Game Awards as Gang of Dragon—although the reveal was really just a brief CGI clip of Ma Dong-Seok that could have been lifted straight from Korean action film The Outlaws.

The wheels came off just a few months later, though, when NetEase pulled funding for the studio, amidst a broader pullback from external studio support over the previous year. Nagoshi Studio reportedly had no success finding another benefactor to fill the gap, and two months later, in May, the studio's website disappeared.

No official proclamations about the fate of the studio were forthcoming, though, and the Steam page remained online, so faint hope of a last-minute rescue persisted. Now, I'm afraid even that's gone, although the Steam listing is still up if you want to poke around at what might have been.

It should come as no surprise that Devens family is still celebrating Rick Devens winning that grand prize money in Big Brother. By all accounts, the brood seems quite ecstatic, and for good reason. To that end, Rick's wife, Becca, decided to use Halloween as a means to pay tribute to her hubby. Becca Devens decided to celebrate Halloween by dressing up the pool float he used the most in the house. #3700. Gay People (Mostly) Explain Gay Halloween

When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of social media the day itself has taken the back seat—it’s online where the battle for the best costumes takes place, and it’s happening earlier every year.

The trend began taking shape in the late 2010s and gained strength during the pandemic: celebrities—most notably the Kardashian-Jenner clan—began re-creating memorable moments from pop culture, mostly old film posters or iconic music album covers, and staging elaborate costume shoots for their Instagrams. The closer the re-creation would get to the original the better—and worthier of likes.

The idea of gay Halloween exists somewhere in this realm, though it’s inevitably more lo-fi, and the most successful looks aim for laughs rather than mere online clout. Plainly, it’s when people—mostly gay men—pick a niche pop culture moment or meme and re-create it in a costume. Forget witches and Scream masks. In 2004, Mean Girls declared, “In girl world, Halloween is the one night of the year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it.” The 2026 equivalent is less about horny devils. Halloween is now the one night of the year when you can let out your inner freak or geek: Now you can be the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, or Marc Jacobs when he wore a neck brace. Two years ago, a friend dressed as Antonio, a character played by Ariana Grande on Saturday Night Live. Another at the same party went as Rihanna as a nun for an Interview magazine cover.

Owen Thiele and Benito Skinner dressed as PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson for Halloween.

Once upon a time, Halloween was about being as frightening as possible. Sure, there is something indeed terrifying about being broken up with via Post-it, and some less-online people are still attached to the classics—a zombie, a devil, et cetera—but Halloween has been co-opted by the internet, and by celebrity culture, in a way that has made it entirely self-indulgent.

Consider Heidi Klum’s famous annual Halloween bash, which she started in 2000. Early on, her costumes evolved from classic (a dominatrix the first year, a vampire in 2005) to more complex (a skinless person in 2011) to complete cosplay. In 2015, Klum appeared as Jessica Rabbit; in 2018, as the ogre version of Fiona from Shrek. Last year, she was a Medusa, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, a hoplite turned into stone. There are Hollywood-level prosthetics, and, largely, it appears as if her costumes are made more for an image than for a party. Klum, in this space, is both the trendsetter and the shining example of the way our collective take on the holiday has evolved to adjust to our online-first lifestyles.

“Someone I just started working with recently said, ‘We live in a reference economy,’” says stylist Ron Hartleben, who works with Camila Cabello and Tyla, among others. “That really struck me,” he says. “Everything has been done. Everyone has access to all the same images now.” So much so that people in the queer community “have gone about seeking the most niche, obscure reference from a show or pop culture moment and making that their Halloween costume” so that a mere mortal, in this case a cis, heterosexual person, may not understand it. “Gay Halloween is exploiting that obscure moment in pop culture and running with it to create one of the most stupid and entertaining outfits imaginable,” Hartleben says. “As long as you think it’s funny and you get it, you’re doing gay Halloween right.” Consider Benito Skinner and Mary Beth Barone’s costume this year as a shining example of gay Halloween: they dressed as Dakota Johnson and Ellen DeGeneres and even recreated their infamous, viral interview about the actor’s birthday party.

But gay Halloween has now broken past its own internet bubble. Celebrities and straight normies alike have adopted the reference-first language popular in queer and adjacent subcultures—from drag to ballroom and beyond—and made it mainstream to come off as more in-the-know.

Last year, Mandy Lee, a trend forecaster known as @oldloserinbrooklyn on TikTok and Instagram, dressed as Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, a video she reposted this year next to the original clip of Anderson to much online buzz (hers was taken by the Gowanus Canal in Brooklyn). “It’s a format that works particularly well online versus IRL because you’re able to [have] text onscreen or even throw up reference images to make it click,” Lee says. She categorizes her costumes as “fashion Halloween,” which she says lives under the same umbrella as gay Halloween. She’s dressed as Lynn Yaeger and Miuccia Prada before, and also the “tabi swiper.” The trick is that they are, as she says, “low effort.” They’re costumes that rely on what’s already in Lee’s closet—no production value, just a sense of humor. “It’s just fun to get hyper specific and granular,” Lee says. “[The costumes] are also not for everyone; they are for fashion people, and that’s what makes it fun.”

Earlier this week, stylist and creative director Chris Horan, who works with the likes of Charli xcx, Demi Lovato, and Christina Aguilera, reposted clips he’d been tagged in on Instagram of fans dressed as Adéla, for whom he is both stylist and creative director. “I obviously love when people dress up or reference any of the looks we’ve worked on,” Horan says. “It takes a lot of effort to make any sort of look on our part or [the fans’], so it always makes me happy to see it.”

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

Last year Horan worked with Lovato on her costume, for which she dressed as Poot Lovato, her fictional twin sister that originated from a Tumblr post in 2015. Poot had long been a gay Halloween staple, but her fans would have never imagined that Lovato herself would bring her back to the forefront in such a way. Horan thinks these costumes also speak to something bigger: “I don’t think you’re really hitting as a pop star if you don’t have an immediately identifiable look.”

The internet has changed the way we do most things, particularly getting dressed, so it’s no surprise that it would affect how we get dressed up. We do things not just for ourselves, or even the people who will see the costume IRL, but for our circles, or “followers,” to congratulate us. Social media may not have ruined Halloween—it’s made it funnier and perhaps less spooky—but it’s altered its spirit.

#3699. New Port Of NFS Underground 2 Turns The Beloved PS2 Racer Into A Wild MMO

It’s a day ending in the letter “Y,” so you know what that means? Yup, another classic video game has been ported in some oddball way with the assistance of AI coding. This time around, someone has gotten PlayStation 2 classic Need for Speed: Underground 2 playable via a web browser, and in this version, you can race alongside dozens of other people at the same time.

Need for Speed: Underground 2 was released back in 2004 and became one of the most popular games of the year thanks to its open-world design and Fast and Furious-like nighttime racing action. It’s like a proto-Forza Horizon, but with a lot more underglow and NOS. And now, thanks to NFS Underground 2 Revived, if you have nostalgic memories of Underground 2 and want to once again drift around its city streets, you can do so in your web browser without having to download a single file or install anything. Oh, and if you want, you can now relive your nostalgia alongside some of the thousands of players currently enjoying this Underground 2 port, according to the site’s data. Just be prepared for some chaos.

My favorite childhood racing game got imported to a website and now 3000 people are free roaming.. this is so fucking funny pic.twitter.com/cUCiz6JDRm

NFSU2 Revived was released late last month, but has recently blown up as fans have discovered the free-to-play browser port via viral clips of the dozens of player-controlled cars smashing into each other on streets that were never designed for this kind of online multiplayer mayhem.Â  Don’t worry, you don’t have to race with others if you just want to enjoy the original solo experience of NSFU2 on your PC in 2026. The multiplayer chaos is opt-in.

The person behind this port claims that they used to play Underground 2 when they were younger, and the creator put this project together so they could “play together again.”

“It worked surprisingly well, and it got a bit out of hand,” said the fan modder and developer. “It’s great to see so many people playing it.”

And as mentioned up top, yes, this port was developed with the help of AI tools, as documented on the Revived’s GitHub page. While I’m not a fan of the AI enshittifcation of the world, it’s also getting harder and harder to play or report on cool game projects and retro mods, like Revived, without running into some amount of AI coding. I’ve talked to numerous devs, big and small, working on these kinds of projects, and for many, these tools are just part of their workflow now.

Now we wait to see if EA, the original publisher of Underground 2, steps in and shuts this all down. Though the company does seem a bit busy right now…

#3698. The Garmin Cirqa Finally Got a Much-Needed Feature

This week Garmin's screenless Cirqa smart band received a firmware update that fixes one of its most obvious gaps: the lack of alerts from your phone. With Version 4.20, you can now set up your smart band to buzz your wrist for texts, calls, and other smart notifications from your phone. The addition is listed on Garmin's forums as "Support vibration for smart notifications/incoming calls." Reaction has been upbeat, too—users on the Garmin subreddit have been glad to see the feature arrive.

Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.

To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.

Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.

Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

Configure notifications in Garmin Connect. Back in Garmin Connect, tap the Menu (or More) tab. Select Garmin Devices, then choose your Cirqa Smart Band. Go to Notifications & Alerts (or Smart Notifications) and turn on text and call alerts.

Troubleshooting tip: If alerts aren't coming through, check that Do Not Disturb, Sleep Mode, and any aggressive Battery Saver settings are turned off on both your phone and the band.

For most a lot of Cirqa fans, the phone alerts are the headline, but the 4.20 update carries a solid list of other improvements and bug fixes:

Trail Run: Run/Walk detection is now available for Trail Run activities.

Timestamp fix: Resolved a problem where an activity's recorded time didn't match the time on your phone.

Distance calibration: You can now calibrate distance for Treadmill Run, Indoor Rowing, and Indoor Cycling before saving the activity on the device.

Duration alerts: Duration time alerts for speaking out now accumulate.

Stress alerts: Stress alerts are now blocked while Auto Activity Detection is recording.

Bedtime reminders: Fixed an issue where the bedtime approaching notification sometimes failed to trigger.

Live Activity: Heart rate now appears on the Live Activity screen before recording begins.

Pinned activity bug: Fixed an issue where the pinned activity reverted to Timed Activity after changing the phone's language.

Workout editing: Fixed a problem that prevented editing reps during a workout.

Stability: General system stability improvements.

It’s been years since I’ve watched Steven Seagal’s only masterpiece, Under Siege. Luckily, the 1992 classic will be available with a Netflix subscription on November 6, and I plan on watching ASAP. It’s the one and only Seagal movie that is truly worth appointment viewing, and that’s for quite a few reasons, like the bonkers cast, the really cool shooting location, and, of course, Seagal at his physical peak (he’s a long way from that today). It should be, in my opinion, considered one of the best action movies of the 1990s.

You really have to kick this conversation off with the incredible cast of Under Siege. It’s rare that there are any other stars in a Seagal movie other than Seagal himself. That’s not true here. Instead of a faceless villain, we get Tommy Lee Jones as William Strannix, a former CIA operative with a serious case of narcissism. Jones is amazing in the role, as he so often is as a bad guy. The scene with Strannix eating roast beef with a chef's knife is peak ‘90s cinema. Usually, Seagal’s foes are two-dimensional, but not here.

Playing Strannix's sidekick is none other than Gary Busey. Sure, Busey doesn’t exactly have the best reputation in 2026, but in 1992, he was still thought of as a great actor, and he’s great here. He’s weaselly and slimy, and so easy to hate. He’s more hateable than Jones, that’s for sure. He’s actually perfect for the role at this point in his career. He’s a little crazy, but not too crazy, and it pays off on screen.

One of the movie's coolest aspects is its setting. At its heart, Under Siege is a heist movie, and Strannix and his band of thieves are targeting missiles on the USS Missouri, intended for the black market, hoping to spark World War III. In that respect, Strannix is basically a Bond villain trying to pull off an audacious crime to set in motion huge global changes. While shooting on the actual USS Missouri, one of the most decorated battleships in US Naval history, would have been tough to set up, they did shoot much of the movie on the USS Alabama, a retired World War II ship.

The Alabama and the Missouri are different class battleships, but they were both built just before or during the war, and are pretty similar. In a normal Seagal movie, you’d expect the whole thing to be filmed on a soundstage in Burbank, but not this one. They used a real ship, and it makes all the difference in how the movie looks. You really feel like you’re on the Missouri in this, and you believe that Seagal’s character, Casey Ryback, is a former Navy SEAL.

Seagal is really at the peak of his powers in Under Siege. He was coming off a wildly successful string of lower-budget action movies in the late ‘80s and early ‘90s, and he was ready for a big-time movie. In a lot of his later films (including Under Siege 2), he’s simply not believable as an unstoppable force, but he is in Under Siege, for sure. Though he’s been out of the spotlight for a long time, I do love going back to those early movies and remembering why Seagal was great and considered one of the biggest action stars of the ‘90s. Under Siege is the number one reason for that.
