Amazon has dropped the price of the 65-inch Toshiba Z670R to $549.97 from $748.99, taking nearly $200 off and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. The deal also includes free delivery to a room of your choice, which normally costs $19.99, though it does not cover unpacking, setup, packaging removal, or haul-away services. You also get a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music with your purchase.

Beyond the discounts, the Z670R has quite a bit going for it, starting with a 4K Mini-LED panel that combines QLED color with local dimming to help bright highlights stand out without washing out darker scenes. It also supports Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+, so you can enjoy compatible HDR content across a wide range of movies, shows, and streaming services.

Gaming is another area where this TV makes a strong case for itself—its panel can run at up to 144Hz, while Variable Refresh Rate, Auto Low Latency Mode, and AMD FreeSync Premium are there to keep fast movement looking smoother and cut down on screen tearing with a compatible console or gaming PC, making it well-suited for racing games, shooters, and sports titles. You also get four HDMI inputs, with support for 4K at 144Hz, so there is room for a console, PC, soundbar, and another device without constantly swapping cables.

Fire TV is built in as well, which means Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, and other major streaming apps are available without adding a separate streaming stick, while Alexa handles voice searches and basic controls. The built-in audio is also more substantial than what you get from many slim TVs, with a dedicated bass woofer and Dolby Atmos support, so you may be able to live without a soundbar at first if you are setting up a bedroom or smaller living room. One potential downside is that Mini-LED does not give you the perfect blacks of OLED, so movie fans who watch mostly in a dark room may still prefer to pay more for one. For someone who splits time between movies, sports, and gaming, though, the Z670R gives you a lot of flexibility for about $550 without immediately requiring extra equipment.

#3694. Overwatch’s Director Explains Why The Same Few Heroes Keep Getting Skins

The distribution of cosmetic skinsâwhich heroes get the lionâs share and which ones get significantly fewerâ is a pretty sensitive subject in the Overwatch community. Years of Mercy, Kiriko, and Juno players constantly eating good while Baptiste, Venture, and Wrecking Ball players wait months if not years for a new Legendary skin have some people jaded about the whole process, with some players even criticizing some of the gameâs base hero designs as feeling like they are made with a âcosmetics-firstâ mindset.

During a group interview Kotaku was present for, game director Aaron Keller talked about the challenges of giving attention to its soon-to-be 55 heroes in not just cosmetics, but in storylines the game has introduced over the gameâs 10 years. He says itâs a problem the team at Blizzard has been dealing with for years, one which he admits is âtrickyâ as the roster grows.

âEvery new piece of content that we introduce to the game, whether it’s a hero or even a map, you know, means that the pool of everything that we’ve got, it is spread out a little bit,â he says. âWe recognize how important it is to continue supporting all of the different heroes in the game. And on one side of it, it’s cosmetics, but as we delve into the story and the narrative for the game, you hear from a lot of players about like, âHey, when is this particular hero going to enter the story?â Or, âIt felt like you kind of left off, let’s say, for example, the story of Zarya years ago. When are you going to pick that thing back up?â And so it definitely makes that more difficult.â

With the introduction of the battle pass and frequent store refreshes, Overwatch is producing more skins in recent years than it used to when the game was primarily supported through loot boxes. Keller says that while the team has to prioritize characters who âsupport the actual bottom-line business,â he hopes that initiatives like creating two customizable Mythic skins per season can allow them to more frequently support heroes that have gotten less love over the years, while also always featuring at least one who typically drives skin sales.

âAs a team we have been, over the past few years, constantly expanding our capacity and our throughput for the amount of skins that we make. And as we do that, it allows us to not just make skins for a lot of the heroes that, if I’m being honest, do more to support the actual bottom-line business for the game,â Keller says. âAnd it also allows us to start making cosmetics for some of our other heroes. The place that you can see that the most transparently is the Mythic skins that we release. Each season we release two Mythic skins, and typically one of those is going to be for a hero that we think is actually going to really drive a lot of that support for the business. And then another one is going to be for a hero that typically hasn’t gotten either a Mythic or a lot of other skins in the recent past. So we recognize it’s important to players. We want to be doing as much of it as we can, but we still always want to be doing it in a way that’s also responsible, and [lets us] know that we can continue supporting this game going forward.â

Overwatch started putting out two Mythic skins per season a year ago in October of 2025, and Iâd say most of the seasons that have followed have adhered to the blueprint Keller describes, featuring one hero who is a tried-and-true seller of skins and another one whoâs gotten less love over the years. Lifeweaver and Junkrat are a good example of a pair of heroes who are on opposite ends of the skin-receiving spectrum, but you also have last season when Genji and Widowmaker both got their second Mythic skins in the same batch, a move which frustrated many players who were waiting for an underserved hero to get the spotlight. The current season, which began on October 6, launched with a Mythic skin for Wuyang, who has received several skins since his launch last year. Weâll see what the second Mythic is when the gameâs midseason phase begins later this week.

Celebrities brought their A-game this Halloween. From Megan Fox going full Twilight as a gothic vampire to Carmen Electra dressing as Catwoman, A-listers truly sought to lean on creativity and individuality when devising their looks for the holiday. As for Jennifer Lopez, she decided to go for a topless look to channel her Monster-In-Law co-star, Jane Fonda, while dressing as the powerful Barbarella.

Jennifer Lopez has proved time and again this year what a fashionista she is. Most recently, she looked dreamy and romantic at Paris Fashion Week wearing a sheer dress and brought fall vibes in a fur coat and sheer, luxe black dress. For Halloween, you couldn’t expect anything less, as her Barberella look was not only fierce but also served as a fitting tribute to one of Jane Fonda's most distinct movie roles. Check it out in the Instagram post below:

For those who don’t know, Barbarella is a campy cult classic that sees Fonda portraying a futuristic female astronaut who encounters strange planets while trying to locate Dr. Durand-Durand. One of the Roger Vadim-directed sci-fi flick’s most memorable qualities is the array of outlandish futuristic costumes that Fonda wears. With that in mind, Lopez couldn’t have picked a better movie to channel for her Halloween costume this year.

The Maid in Manhattan actress is showing the right to bear arms while wearing Barbarella’s mesh silver-laced dress with metallic boots. I’m also loving the white bodysuit with the black vertical stripes running down. The ‘60s blonde wig she’s wearing as the aforementioned character is such a nice nod to the decade and fictional space heroines in general.

And Lopez can’t celebrate the cult classic’s sexual liberation theme without taking a topless photo of herself, which sees her posing with blind angel Pylar. All in all, JLo looks like she’s having a lot of fun honoring her former co-star’s psychedelic movie.

With how on-point Jennifer Lopez looks as Barbarella, you’d think she was auditioning for the remake of the 1968 film. I mean, she’s wearing each outfit with such pizzazz and poise. However, Sydney Sweeney is set to “save the universe” as the film's lead. The actress seems like a great fit, and I'm confident she'll do a great job embodying the iconic space adventurer.

Per what's known about the remake, Edgar Wright has been in talks to direct, while Kingsman's Jane Goldman and Honey Ross have also been approached to write the screenplay. While the upcoming science-fiction movie is still in its development stages, it’s great that the “On the Floor” singer is already bringing the movie back into the general public's consciousness.

When it comes to the long line of costumes Jennifer Lopez has worn for Halloween over the years, these Barbarella looks may be amongst my favorites. If anything, now I'd like to know how Jane Fonda feels about her former co-star paying tribute to her and her character. In the meantime, anyone who's curious and wants to check out Barbarella can do so by watching the movie for free on Pluto TV.

#3692. Unpacking Nicki Minaj’s MAGA Style Evolution

This is the October 28, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

Pieter Mulier’s Versace debut will be marked with a couture show and the runway revival of Atelier Versace in January, and Bottega Veneta is back on Instagram for the first time since 2021—pouring one out to the fan accounts that had been enjoying their window of opportunity. Otherwise, the fashion news cycle has taken a break so far this week, so I’ve turned my attention to the midterm elections. Below, find missives on Nicki Minaj’s Gucci skirt suit by Demna—which was not provided to her by the brand—and the old style trick the Dems have adopted to appeal to us common folk. Plus, I get into why people love to clown Drake for his outfits. (For the record, I thought his Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed cape was fabulous.)

I wrote this edition of Fit Check wearing a sequined ghost costume (a ghost writer, get it?). It was my attempt at finding the right mindset to unpack what the internet has dubbed “gay Halloween,” for which I enlisted some of my fellow friends of Dorothy, and other experts, to help explain the formerly niche, now very viral internet phenomenon.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff, Ralph Lauren, Bailey Moon, Juliet Charlotte, Marc Jacobs, Ariana Grande, Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, and many more.

“These Dem men with their hiked sleeves are taking me out,” read a comment under a clip of Senator Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg on TikTok. “So hot.”

Ossoff and Buttigieg are the latest notable adopters of what appears to be the Democratic sartorial strategy for the ongoing midterm elections: to roll up their sleeves, literally. In a stark contrast to the most visible men on the right, who are all properly suited up both on the Hill in Washington, DC, and out on the campaign trail, “Dem men,” including Barack Obama and Gavin Newsom, have all been sporting a more casual look while campaigning. Individually, there’s nothing particular about the look. Obama and Buttigieg are former government officials; they’re technically off duty. Ossoff seems to want to position himself as a man of the people, and Newsom is working on embodying the anti-Trump. And yet, when seen together, the Dem men seem to have all agreed in a group chat to look a bit more working-class. No meticulously tailored Ralph Lauren suits, just dudes at work.

“There is a certain formula for cultivating a relaxed, approachable image while campaigning, versus the more polished presentation that comes with actually holding office,” says stylist Bailey Moon, who consulted with Dr. Jill Biden and Joe Biden during their time at the White House and worked with Tim Walz on the campaign trail in 2024. “It’s amusing to me, the idea that exposing your forearms suddenly makes you a man of the people, but rolling up your sleeves has become a political and metaphorical shorthand for being hardworking, accessible, and ready to get it done,” he says.

So is there a Dem men ’fit-pic group chat? “I don’t think there’s a coordinated effort,” Moon says. “I do think that politicians respond to a certain visual vocabulary, and right now, in a bid to win back working-class voters, that vocabulary is less formal and more familiar.”

Politicians do, in fact, think about their clothes more than we might think. “The visual language is always considered, even when the clothing itself isn’t front and center,” Moon says. “The challenge is making that feel instinctive rather than rehearsed, which ultimately comes down to the principal (key player) and how they carry it.” Ossoff et al. may not be folding up their sleeve cuffs as a joint campaign effort, and they may not be doing so to invoke some thirst in the comments section, but they’re making choices.

Drake celebrated his 40th birthday in New York City last weekend wearing black leather pants, a black turtleneck, and a brown fringed cape that got everyone talking. The rapper became the punch line of the weekend online before his outerwear piece was revealed as being a design by Martin Margiela during his time at Hermès—an archival holy grail find that Drake’s stylist, Juliet Charlotte, sourced from Canadian vintage seller Alex Maxamenko. He was called “Pumpkin Spice Papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle, @champagnepapi. He was compared to the Real Housewives venturing to Aspen on a girls trip. He was described as a rich auntie, and, my favorite, as ready for “Christian-girl autumn.”

The jokes were admittedly quite funny, and as we get into the “gay Halloween” phenomenon below, actor and comedian Sima Sepehri has already turned the viral moment into her costume. Yet underneath the surface of this mostly good-spirited fun—and my apologies for being the fun police—lies a layer of homophobia and, yes, misogyny. Drake has long been a punch line in the music industry and within hip-hop. People online have mocked him for the decor of his home and suggested he’d had a BBL or was showing off fake abs. He’s been called a wuss, and, pardon my French, a pussy. Which is where the issues with his style becoming a punch line begin.

Most of the jokes around Drake’s style compare him to women—to white women and their keenness for the fall season, to rich reality TV stars, to family matriarchs, and more. It’s simply too easy to call Drake and his penchant for fashion “feminine” or “fruity,” as if most famous men today, from his fellow rappers to athletes and actors, didn’t share his same affection for fashion and style. In a way, it’s not that serious. (And how he wore the shawl did look like he belonged more at a ski chalet than in the city.) Except that it kind of is; we have somehow not been able to shake gay as a zinger, and that’s generally because, culturally, we still consider femininity—and therefore women—to be less than masculinity and manliness. Let Drake wear his shawl. You’ve paid for it with your streams.

President Donald Trump and Nicki Minaj at a campaign event in Michigan.

President Trump made headlines last week for his comments on Senator Jon Husted’s physique, particularly his rear end. But he wasn’t done. This week, Trump attempted to crack a joke about it. “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” the president said on Sunday at a Republican campaign rally in Michigan. “That’s hard to miss,” he said, before looking at the rapper and instructing her to “stand up!” Minaj did, and waved to the crowd and the president as if thanking him for the…uh, compliment.

Minaj has been a puzzling character to watch as she ventures deeper into the MAGA-sphere—she’s even been jokingly floated as a potential next White House press secretary. (Minaj held a mock interview about Trump aboard Air Force One, which was posted to X by White House communications director Steven Cheung with the caption, “Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House press secretary! @NICKIMINAJ.”)

On Sunday, the rapper was wearing a skirt suit by Gucci, retailing for about $4,000. Her look was finished with Pink Friday press-on nails, her own brand, and matching Gucci-logo pumps. In a way, the outfit is a departure from what one usually sees onstage at MAGA rallies, where luxury fashion—and particularly logos—rarely reign supreme unless coming from the first lady. Minaj, unlike other Trump acolytes, is often clad in on-trend designer clothes (when she joined President Trump at the Treasury Department Trump Accounts Summit in January of this year, she was wearing an Alaïa dress by Pieter Mulier), and while the idea of a prim skirt suit certainly suggested she was dressed for business, or at least for politics, the loud, allover monogram logo felt like a remnant of the musical superstar that was, or that remains somewhere underneath the surface.

As for what this means for Gucci, its clients likely won’t find the image of Minaj deterring—it’s not like the brand is underwriting Minaj’s appearance or the messaging around it. But perhaps the image of Minaj onstage will inspire the MAGA set to adopt Demna’s revamp of the house—some of the caricatural archetypes in his most recent collection certainly leaned conservative. Funnily enough, Karlie Kloss, wife of Josh Kushner and sister-in-law to Jared, wore a similar pencil skirt at Demna’s first Gucci runway show.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K in half, dropping it to $29.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers, with a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music included in the purchase. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $10. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $30.

#3690. Suda51 Wants A Now-Independent Grasshopper To Bring Back No More Heroes (And One Of His Earliest Games)

Grasshopper ManufactureNetEaseNo More Heroes

Grasshopper Manufacture, now independent of Netease Games as of the beginning of October, has been seeking to define what its trajectory will be without the benefit of that financial backing. Suda51, the studio’s founder, sat down with a number of Japanese outlets to discuss the future of the company, how plans have changed since it went independent, and the future of its No More Heroes series.

According to Suda51, one of the biggest shifts that will occur as a result of this independence and lack of financial backing is in the scale of the games the studio will be capable of developing. Under NetEase, the company had promised to develop three large games within 10 years, with February’s Romeo Is a Dead Man being one of these.Â These plans will have to be adapted, he explains in an interview with 4Gamer. âThat was a plan we made based on a promise given to NetEase at the time, so that will have to change,â he said, adding, âAs an independent studio itâs now possible to take on various jobs. I want to not just work on my own titles, but also on various interesting IPs.â Speaking to Famitsu in a separate interview, he even mentions two series heâd love to work with: Mobile Suit Gundam and Marvelâs Deadpool.

Suda51 admits that itâs a difficult time to become independent. The company handled promotion and the release of Romeo Is a Dead Man in-house, even though it had initially been planned as a NetEase work. Speaking to 4Gamer, he says promoting the title was a challenge for the studio because of how the industry has evolved in recent years. âRaising awareness for a game is really difficult,â he admits. âThatâs because compared to the old promotion, PR and marketing cycle, this era is completely different. Before, it was a challenge over how many TV commercials you could do, how much you were advertising in magazines or online. But thatâs not the case anymore.â To counter the challenges of advertising in the modern era, the studio hopes to take advantage of the Grasshopper brand to some extent. âWeâve been a studio for around 30 years, and our name has even become recognizable overseas to a point, and Iâve realized that there has to be a way we can use that and make more use of our brand power.â

As it looks to the future, the company is examining platforms, including Roblox, as a way to allow it toÂ  experiment with ideas, and it’s actively recruiting new members to the team. Earlier this year, to mark the release of Romeo Is a Dead Man, the company held a demo event in Shibuya PARCO, a department store in Tokyo, where it proudly announced that another new game would be releasing this year. While that hasnât come to fruition, Suda51 is insisting this unknown game will be released next year.

In his conversation with Famitsu, he was more specific about what he wanted to create next. âI have a few ideas of what to make next, but one thing Iâm thinking about is a game I made while I was still at Human, called Moonlight Syndrome. That was the game that started my career, and from there I made The Silver Case, Flower, Sun and Rain and Killer7. I really want to channel that idea once again if I can. I think No More Heroes has given many people the impression of Grasshopper as a bright and flashy action game studio, but I want to return to the side of the studio that specializes in the dark, serious, and chaotic ideas that we worked on until Killer7.â

Notably, Moonlight Syndrome, released by Human Entertainment in 1997 for PlayStation, has yet to be officially released overseas. At the very least Suda hopes to make this work an international release at last. And perhaps a return to No More Heroes is also in the cards. Speaking about Marvelous, which owns the No More Heroes IP, he said the company is “very aware [that next year is the 20th anniversary of No More Heroes], so Iâd love for us to do something to mark the occasion. Iâm hoping to do something special, so please look forward to it. Travis Touchdown is definitely coming back!â

Based on these interviews, it seems that the now-independent Grasshopper Manufacture is a studio that wishes to look back, as well as look to the future. While its plans have changed since it first signed with NetEase, it wants to at least stick to the intent it previously had, if not at quite the same scale, while creating things that fans of the studio will enjoy.

Nightdive has unveiled the first trailer for Thief: The Tarnished Mirror, a new official expansion to Thief coming with its imminent remaster. Most exciting of all: The Tarnished Mirror is being made by the team behind The Black Parade, a 2023 mod that was one of the most exciting things to happen to the series in 20 years.

The Tarnished Mirror consists of four new missions, and is meant "as a bridge between Thief: The Dark Project and Thief 2: The Metal Age," according to an accompanying press release. Similar to The Black Parade, these new levels will leverage improvements in technology to offer more sprawling, ambitious maps than '90s PCs could handle.

The scenes from the trailer are all very Thief, but similar to The Black Parade, there's immediately more verticality than in the 1997 original game. There are also glimpses at interiors that leverage familiar Thief assets to create weirder, more surprising spaces than I'm used to from the mainline games.

The press release also indicates that The Tarnished Mirror will embrace Thief's contested legacy of horror in a similar way to The Black Parade, and that's music to my ears. I've always been a Thief undead mission defender, and The Black Parade upped the ante⁠—it's one of the scariest games I've ever played.

All told, this news about the expansion has more than made up for my disappointment at there being no PC version of the remaster's big box special edition. I may not get my tchotchke fix here, but the Thief Remaster is shaping up to be something very special.

Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything has been stirring up buzz and earning its fair share of money. However, one honor that had been alluding it was the No. 1 spot at the box office. Well, that's no longer the case, as the doc finally became the top movie in the United States this weekend. And regardless of whether that win can be attributed to people showing up because of all the Oscar buzz, or the scene that literally shows everything, it's also resulted in the documentary obtaining a very rare honor.

It should be mentioned that Fielder's film just barely won the top spot, as Warner Bros. and DC Studios' Clayface just missed winning Halloween weekend after its strong start by a little less than $200,000. Wildwood, which some are calling one of the best and scariest movies of the year, remains in third place this week, while steamy fantasy flick Wicker climbed another spot too. Check out the full breakdown below:

6. BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Buenos Aires and São Paulo Live Viewing

9. The Only Living Pickpocket In New York

The No. 1 spot aside, this is a truly auspicious moment for You Can See Everything, because in a rare turn of events, it's now the fourth documentary ever to win a weekend box office. With that, it now joins Fahrenheit 9/11, Michael Jackson's This Is It and Taylor Swift: The Official Release Of A Showgirl. That's a lineup even more wtf than some of the moments in the film. Nevertheless, this is quite the distinction for Fielder and co.

I Wondered Why Nathan Fielder Was Picked For You Can See Everything. His Answer Confused Me

One way YCSE differentiates itself from this lineup, however, is by having a different path to this milestone. All three of the other movies managed to win the box office in their opening weekends. You Can See Everything opened at No. 2 at the box office weeks ago and held that spot last week before finally grabbing the top spot this week.

Whether Fielder's film will hold that spot again next week remains to be seen. Clayface is still sticking around, and it had about 200 more theaters screening the body horror thriller this weekend. That comic book film is already proving to be a solid win for DC, as it has grossed roughly $83 million worldwide against a reported budget between $30 and $44 million.

Plus, a new month means a new slate of films arriving on the 2026 movie schedule. The Cat in the Hat and Godzilla Minus Zero are among the titles arriving in a week's time, and there's always the chance that they could shake things up at the B.O. next week.

All this to say, I expect You Can See Everything to stick around the Top 10 for at least a few more weeks based on how it's trending. I'm very curious as to just how much longer it'll continue to haul in millions, as I don't know if anyone saw this run coming. I'm just hoping to hear that this means Nathan Fielder is going to get more documentaries in theaters, which I would absolutely love to see.

#3687. Nick Fuentes Opts Out of the 2026 Midterms, Unlike Fellow Livestreamer Hasan Piker

It was a little after 4:30 in the morning this past June when Andy O’Brian says he jolted awake to muffled banging on the door of his Los Angeles home. As he came face-to-face with close to a dozen LAPD officers, O’Brian had a hunch about who’d sent them and why. Moments later, one of the officers asked O’Brian: “Are you trying to kill a guy named Nick?”

The sheriffs that morning wouldn’t likely have known that the “Nick” in question was a reference to Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white supremacist streamer with some 1.2 million followers on X and one of the largest streaming audiences on the conservative news platform Rumble. They were even less likely to know that O’Brian, a longtime follower of Fuentes—or a “groyper,” as the faithful like to call themselves—says he was swatted because he recently questioned the streamer’s political tactics in a group chat.

“Usually the right fucks with people on the left,” O’Brian tells me on a phone call this past September. “But now the right is fucking with people on the right. Like, how do I explain to the cops that [they’d been called because] I’m not Nazi enough?”

In the world of anonymous online accounts that orbit Fuentes and share his radical “America First” political agenda, O’Brian was a central figure at just 21. Better known by his online handle, Chad Champion, he’d watched Fuentes’s streams from age 14, following him from platform to platform as he was continually banned. O’Brian started posting himself and grew into a far-right microcelebrity. He soon found himself welcomed into Fuentes’s small inner circle, the “groyper generals.”

But it’s not exactly clear where this so-called army is marching. With his increasingly massive following, Fuentes is positioned to be a kingmaker in conservative politics. He’s long spoken of remaking the Republican Party, and he seems to control a loyal voting bloc populated by one of the most coveted demographics in electoral politics right now: young men. But the culture O’Brian describes to me doesn’t sound like a vanguard of white nationalism or anything close to a political organizing operation like the Democratic Socialists of America. Rather, it sounds like most online communities: transient spaces anchored by a celebrity-like figurehead, in this case Fuentes, who, according to O’Brian, was more concerned with gaming and earning money from his nightly streams than true politicking. (A recent report in The Washington Post estimated he earned nearly $900,000 from “superchat” donations between early 2025 and March 2026.) Each night, after Fuentes’s shows on Rumble ended, O’Brian says a select few would be invited to play Fortnite with the influencer.

FAR FAR RIGHT Fuentes provided extreme-right counter-programming to Turning Point USA’s “The People’s Convention” in Detroit, Michigan, June 15, 2024.

The community is highly deferential to Fuentes, O’Brian says, eager to gain his favor by clipping and posting moments from his show or attacking his critics online. It can verge into sycophancy as groypers grow consumed with “glazing” the leader, O’Brian adds, to the point that Fuentes has come to resent his own movement. “He hates all of those people,” O’Brian says, referring to Fuentes, “and everyone in the inner circle hated me because I wasn’t dick-riding him.” (Fuentes, when reached for comment, says: “I hate some of them, definitely.”)

But the real problems started for Chad Champion when things moved from online spaces to electoral politics. Earlier this year, Fuentes chose to endorse James Fishback, a groyper-adjacent character who’d embarked on a longshot bid to become Florida’s next governor. Polling at the time had Fishback in the single to low double digits. It was a test for Fuentes’s real-world clout, and it didn’t go well: Fishback went on to win just 10% of the Republican primary vote this past August.

O’Brian voiced his dissent in a relatively small groyper group chat—“the Chadites”—and his heresy was swiftly leaked to the broader community. “Nick is burning his reputation over this dude,” read one of O’Brian’s texts about Fishback. Fuentes was furious, says O’Brian: “Nick told me I was creating ‘problems’ for him.” Soon after, according to O’Brian, Fuentes called him “disloyal” and targeted him in his Telegram chat as an “antifa” collaborator. (Fuentes denies ever targeting O’Brian or labeling him “antifa.”) Soon after came the swatting.

While O’Brian challenged Fuentes, others have been menaced by his followers simply for trying to build public-facing careers as members of his movement, which has no apparent goals in electoral politics as a seismic midterm election cycle plays out. Unlike a certain political influencer from the opposite side of the spectrum, Hasan Piker, who’s ventured out across the country to harness his influence in service of leftist challengers in Democratic primaries, Fuentes has made little effort to insert himself or his online movement into the physical places where the messy work of political organizing unfolds. Mostly, he seems content to sit on stream in his basement, often describing his viewers as “incels” and “retards” while he rakes in their donations.

It’s left many in this world wondering what exactly Fuentes is chasing: Mainstream approval? Power? Online clout? Dollars? Pure chaos? Does he simply feel the tide going out on Trumpism in his young audience? When I reached out to see if Fuentes would like to comment on this story, he first replied over text: “Groyper gossip? Boooooo.” A few hours later, however, Fuentes called me to offer a more thorough response.

It wasn’t always like this. For some young conservative men, Fuentes’s America First movement became a far-right oasis over the last decade, a taboo-shattering community connecting through irony-pilled memes and a desire to aggressively reshape the American right.

To most outsiders, Fuentes’s vision is a horrifying glimpse at the most mutated strain of conservatism on the political spectrum, one shot through with sneering expressions of white nationalism, antisemitism, race science, and misogyny. There’s cheering approval for Adolf Hitler and fascism in general. In the past year alone, Fuentes has suggested that women are “the number one political enemy in America,” that America needs a “dictator,” that Black people “cannot actually sound out words,” and that political asylum seekers are “illiterate peasants.” In October, Vice President JD Vance seemed to reference Fuentes’s long-running hostility toward his wife, Usha, an Indian American. “Theres this podcaster, who goes obsessively at me and my family,” he said. Fuentes responded by calling Vance an anti-gay slur. When it leaked that he’d sat down for dinner with Donald Trump and Kanye West in 2022, the reports created a massive scandal for the former-and-future president. And when Fuentes and a crew of manosphere influencers including Andrew Tate and Clavicular were captured singing along to West’s “Heil Hitler” at a South Beach nightclub this past January, it was the reactionary right on parade.

Fuentes was born in Chicagoland in 1998 and was something of a typical conservative growing up. But he proved a formidable communicator of extreme ideas while attending Boston University, where in 2017 he launched the show that would make his name: America First With Nicholas J. Fuentes. He attended the Unite the Right Rally in Charlottesville a few months later, dropped out of school soon after that, and became a professional purveyor of far-right vitriol.

YOUTH GROUP As an 18-year-old Boston University student, Fuentes showed up to a protest against Trump's travel ban on January 30, 2017.

He was eventually banned from Twitter (as well as YouTube, Twitch, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit), and his podcast was removed from Spotify for hate-speech violations. But his 2024 reinstatement on Elon Musk’s X has mainstreamed Fuentes’s words and clips. His post crudely mocking a liberal slogan to mark Trump’s victory in that year’s election—“Your body, my choice”—became one of the most viewed political posts of all time. Ever since he appeared on Tucker Carlson’s show last fall, Fuentes has become a kind of mythic figure in conservative circles, representing both the future of the right and all that has seemingly gone awry. This past week, HBO’s John Oliver devoted a large part of a segment to Fuentes’s growing reach. “Fuentes has been inching closer and closer to mainstream Republicans over the years,” he said.

But even as the young men with whom Fuentes has influence begin to sour on the president, discerning the streamer’s political goals is increasingly difficult. Over the course of Trump’s second term, Fuentes has mostly played the part of surly dissident, whipping up controversy between the right’s wobbly coalitions. He’s been openly antagonistic toward the Trump administration, and perhaps the most consistent message he’s conveyed to his followers this past year has been the abandonment of the GOP altogether, urging them to “vote Democrat.” For the Ohio governor’s race, one of the rare contests that Fuentes has directly commented on, he’s come out in support of a female Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, over her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian American entrepreneur who is a frequent target for the white nationalist right.

Meanwhile on X, many of Fuentes’s posts read like lusty-sounding fantasies about the coming onslaught awaiting Republicans this midterm election cycle. “I can’t wait for Republicans to get destroyed in the midterms and then everyone in the admin to be impeached,” reads one Fuentes post. His increasingly nihilistic streams often veer into political incoherence: He continues to engage in extreme racism and misogyny, said it would have been “better” for Kamala Harris to win in 2024 (to supposedly pave the way for “an American Hitler”), and now maintains the Trump administration is a “criminal enterprise.” His public statements have been laced with melancholy too. This spring he wrote in one post on X: “I’m getting really sick of politics honestly.”

For much of the past year, reports of doxxing, sustained harassment campaigns, and occasional swattings within Fuentes’s far-right faction have grown. These tactics once seemed reserved for the group’s perceived enemies on the outside, but they’ve increasingly become a way to punish or banish groypers deemed disloyal to Fuentes. Earlier this year, after CNN aired an interview with two men who self-identified as groypers, Fuentes brutally mocked the pair on stream—criticizing them for, among other things, their normie footwear. In the ensuing pile-on, both were savagely harassed across social media platforms, with groypers even calling for them to be doxxed.

Then there’s the more drastic case of Amy Dangerfield. A former “groypette” and content creator, Dangerfield earned the ire of Fuentes and his generals for the sin of attempting to organize a conference of America First politicians and streamers this past May. Her goal, she claimed at the time, was to bring Fuentes’s political agenda into the real world, and she invited a coalition of right- and left-leaning politicians and influencers to hash out the idea of an “America First” political agenda. The attempt backfired massively. On his Telegram channel, Fuentes claimed that Dangerfield was trying to subvert him, and referred to her as “Amy Dangerslut.”

PROTAGONIST Fuentes has been accused of running a cult of personality without real political goals.

The claim led to a torrent of stomach-churning abuse and harassment directed at Dangerfield and her husband. A story in The Washington Post described how a flood of torture images and doctored content were unleased against the former Fuentes devotee, all because she hadn’t received his blessing to stage a public event. Today, Dangerfield has largely stepped back from far-right politics and her once-promising streaming career.

For years, Fuentes has claimed that his primary objective is the slow takeover of the Republican Party. He often boasts that the groypers are “inside” the institutions of government, and recent reports in the media have traced how Fuentes’s ideas have permeated the young Republican cadre working in Congress and establishment think tanks such as the Heritage Foundation. Fuentes himself likes to brag about the fellow travelers he says are working within the Trump administration, and O’Brian tells me that he’s heard from groypers in DC that Fuentes has traveled there on occasion to meet with his young allies who work in the White House.

But many on the far right find this slow-burn strategy to be a fantasy—or cover for Fuentes’s unwillingness to take larger political risks. Some believe he actually wants to change lanes.

“I think that he saw that the market opened up following the assassination of Charlie Kirk, which is why he’s coming after everyone who is questioning that narrative,” Dangerfield says when I call her up to ask her thoughts. She’s referring to Fuentes’s clashes with Candace Owens over who killed Kirk and why. “I just think he wants to make his money and go mainstream.”

More sympathetic observers on the right think Fuentes’s disinterested approach to electoral politics is a deliberate choice. Aidan Thompson, who’s behind the widely read America First news platform, AF Post, tells me that Fuentes is holding back out of a sense of “responsibility” to his audience and a refusal to support a flawed GOP slate of candidates.

“I think Nick is tapping out because Trump and the party have just totally fucked him off,” Thompson says. “Like, why would you show up?”

When I eventually get Fuentes on the phone, he takes that tack. “I’ve been very open about why I’m not supporting Trump, and that’s because he started a war with Iran,” he says, claiming that many of his predictions about the second Trump presidency have ultimately come true: the war; a perceived failure to follow through on mass deportations; and that the administration is stocked with neoconservatives, America First’s internecine enemies on the right. “All of those things came to fruition,” Fuentes tells me.

He dismisses criticisms that he’s simply sitting out the midterms or trying to poison the GOP’s chances. “People say I’m just sour grapes over Trump or Peter Thiel,” he says, referencing reports that he pitched the latter for funding and failed. “But I’m very open about my problems with these people. It’s all ideological.” Fuentes goes on to explain his strategy is an attempt to correct a “generational mistake” by previous America First candidates like Pat Buchanan, whose followers ultimately lined up behind the Republican Party. Fuentes has instructed his followers to withhold their votes, estimating that this bloc could add up to some 3% of the general election vote. “We can exercise the veto, and I think that’s the source of our power,” he says.

As the midterms drag on with a sense of grinding doom for Republicans, all that might be too conceptual for a younger generation of conservatives hungry to see a far-right takeover of the party. Will Fuentes and his movement stay stuck on the internet, or can they break out? For her part, Dangerfield suggests the failed Fishback endorsement was evidence that Fuentes doesn’t have the “political pull he thinks he does,” while O’Brian is more blunt still: “He clearly can’t be the guy to take things to the next level.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Every time you're testing out a new technology you don't really know how people will react to it. We'd seen some similar reactions with The Finals, we had used a similar technology, so I knew that we were heading into a bit of potential rocky territory. I think there was some really fair criticism in there. There's no point in trying to be defensive, it's just what's best for the game at the end of the day." via Arc Raiders' YouTube channel.

The start of Arc Raiders was a very mixed bag. On one hand it managed to attract an unbelievable amount of players as Embark Studios struck gold with its gentler take on extraction shooters. But all of this hype was somewhat overshadowed by the controversy surrounding its use of AI to mimic voice actors and supplement the dialogue.

While the actors involved did sign contracts allowing Embark to do this, there was still a great deal of backlash from players who were frustrated to see AI injected into the game. Many players pointed out, rightfully so, just how lifeless, lacklustre, and odd some of the AI voicelines sounded, a fact that was made all the more apparent by how fantastic Marathon's NPCs were.

Embark's devs have pointed out, however, that it only used AI in order to get updates out the door faster; that this was due to efficiency rather than an affinity for the technology. "[The actors] have been here all along," Embark's audio director Bence Pajor says. "But we haven't always used them to record the actual thing you're going [to hear] because that's only been solidified super late. We made a lot of training data from their voices so we could prototype as well with their voice.

"Every new item that appears in the game, every new feature, everything needs to have a lot of dialogue because you can ping it. There's so much going into everything. To record the training data for the ping system becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. I mean the actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that. That's not feasible because the game has been changing so fast and we can't call them in every time we just change a feature."

Since the controversy first erupted, Embark has stressed multiple times that it wants to support voice actors. "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually quite the opposite we should celebrate the performance and give them more space," chief creative officer Stefan Strandberg says. "And that is something that I'm hoping to bring to players over the coming years for Arc Raiders: really seeing what the characters are like and who they are, and what motivates them, making it real."

Arguably, though, the damage has already been done. Using AI to bulk up voice lines may be easier, and replacing it with real voice actors when you can is certainly better than the alternative, but it has still set a bad precedent for voice actors in an industry which is relentless in its attempt to cut creative corners to optimise costs.

#3685. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Link’s Tunic Looks Like That Because He Made It Himself

The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

When the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake was first revealed, one of the most common gut reactions I saw across the internet was in response to the game’s overall visual style. And everyone seemed to focus on one thing in particular: Link’s clothes.

Basically, Link’s clothes feature a ridiculous amount of detail. They appear to be hand-woven out of some sort of fiber, and you can see every stitch. There’s a fringe around the bottom, and larger stitches where the sleeves attach and where his hat comes together. Over his tunic, he’s wearing some sort of leather armor with swirling leaf designs. Adult Link’s boots have similar etchings. It all looks…not hyperrealistic or anything, but it certainly has an over-the-top amount of intricacy that the Nintendo 64 Link never could have dreamed of.

There was debate, though, as to whether this was good or not. Some people compared it to the look of Unreal Engine fan games, which have been oft-mocked for missing the simplistic charm of typical Nintendo games. A lot of people felt that Link stood out from his surroundings, especially when he stood next to other NPCs with less detail, such as some folks in Castle Town. But others really liked the tunic and its details, and noted how well it spoke to Link’s origins as a child of the forest.

Well according to the game’s developers, that history is exactly what they were tapping into with the tunic’s intricate look. In an Ask the Developer interview today, art director Aya Shida and producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained how the tunic (and the rest of the art style) came to be. Shida begins by saying the team didn’t take changing the designs lightly, and began by making sketches of the characters to place side-by-side with the old designs, as well as a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree. “We wanted characters like these to blend naturally into a world like this.”

The sketches made by the team don’t look more realistic than the old designs. But the original designs did have significant limits placed upon them by the Nintendo 64’s technology, as Fujibayashi explains:

Back when games were being developed for Nintendo 64, there were limits to what could be expressed in-game. With those limitations in mind, the developers chose to exaggerate the charactersâ movements and defining features so that their distinctive qualities would come through. But if we recreated all of that precisely with today’s technology, it might look a little creepy. (Laughs) I imagine it was quite a challenge to strike the right balance while still preserving each character’s individuality.

Fujibayashi ends by noting that in the new game, there was a lot of attention given to clothing textures now that those limitations have been removed. As an example, Shida offers Young Link’s outfit.

If the fabric looked too neat, as though it had been machine-woven, it wouldn’t look like something the children living in the forest had made themselves. It just wouldn’t feel believable.

So we started by asking what kind of fabric those children might actually weave and wear. We looked at materials in museums and even experimented with making our own fabric from thread to get a better sense of what it should be like. For this game, the hardware allowed us to depict that level of detail, but that also meant we needed to do our research until we had a clear idea of what we wanted to create. As a design team, we often talked about imagining the story behind every object in the game as we created it.

So essentially, while Link’s smooth tunic was fine for the Nintendo 64’s capabilities, on the souped-up Switch 2, a smooth tunic might have looked ridiculous on him and the other Kokiri given what we know about their lore. So instead, the team did a bunch of (frankly very cool) research to work out what sort of clothing would make sense for him and his brethren, clothing which would naturally be quite different from what everyone outside the forest was wearing.

The rest of the interview is pretty cool and worth reading, though if you’re just looking for highlights, you can read real quick about Eiji Aonuma adding, and then removing, more fast travel points to the game. A second part to the interview will be out tomorrow, and the remake of Ocarina of Time is out later this week, on November 5.

I've been a big fan of comedian Grace Reiter since I first saw her on TikTok, and her recent addition to the Saturday Night Live cast has only elevated her star power. I was excited to see she's a part of streaming comedy doing well, as those with a Netflix subscription are finding out about Minimum Wage.

The series follows the young employees of "The Slice Club," a pizza franchise operating across the United States. It all kicks off when Randall Park's Terry Sylvester shows up for an impromptu visit as the company's CEO. I was psyched to see Park in the series and eager to see how the show developed, so I was disappointed when the series largely went on without acknowledging him.

I hadn't gotten enough of Randall Park on the 2026 TV schedule, and I don't have enough of him on Minimum Wage. The pilot sets the stage perfectly with his introduction, and even ends with him moving into the basement of the pizza shop, determined to turn around the lowest-performing store's numbers.

He then proceeds to appear in very little of the series from that point onward. It's baffling considering he is such a television staple, and it almost gives the impression that he was shoehorned into the series at the late stages in order to give Minimum Wage a bit more star power. He never really has as much screen time as he does in the first episode, and most scenes after are only a couple of minutes long.

We have no idea if future seasons of Minimum Wage are part of Netflix's upcoming schedule. If it does return, however, I would humbly request that Randall Park's Terry Sylvester have a larger role in the show than he did in Season 1.

The One Thing Matthew Perry's Sister Loves About The Netflix Documentary Telling Her Brother's Story

To me, the fun in this show is a bunch of teens awkwardly dealing with a middle-aged man experiencing a midlife crisis. While I did enjoy the workplace antics and some of the downsides of serving a room full of theater kids, I feel like the well for content on that can only go so deep.

I do question if Grace Reiter's Saturday Night Live schedule will allow her to continue to commit time to Minimum Wage if it returns for another season. It does seem like more SNL stars than ever are popping up in projects while also doing the show, rather than striking off on their own after a couple of years. I think it has potential, provided they can tweak the series a bit to include more of Randall Park.

Watch Minimum Wage on Netflix right now, as well as all of the other great shows on the platform! I'm still obsessed with The Boroughs despite it being cancelled, and come to think of it, maybe it would've benefitted from having Randall Park involved as well.

Unlike the first season, Cyberpunk: Edgerunners IIâs story takes place after the events of Cyberpunk 2077. As such, fans have been looking throughout the anime for any sign of characters from CD Projekt Redâs RPG, including V, the customizable protagonist the player inhabits. However, since the show takes place post-2077, Vâs appearance would open up a whole messy box of questions about the showâs continuity and whether the broader Cyberpunk franchise now has a âcanonâ ending from the choice-driven game it will adhere to in stories set after Vâs adventures. In fact, those questions have already been raised, and according to showrunner Bartosz Sztybor, thereâs no intention of canonizing or invalidating any of the gameâs potential endings.

In an interview with IGN, Sztybor talked about what some fans believe to have been a V cameo in the new Edgerunners season, specifically of the âdefaultâ female V with a red undercut seen in the gameâs promotional artwork. The personâs face appears in an Arasaka database alongside other cyberware-compatible individuals (including Edgerunners season one protagonist David Martinez), and though the show doesnât make a big to-do about this person specifically, some fans are taking this as a sign that V is alive and in Night City in a post-2077 timeline. However, Sztybor says that any such read of the show is just fan speculation.

âWe don’t want to set a canon ending,âÂ  he says. âSo there were a lot of conversations again with the lore team to see what we can do to somehow satisfy all the endings, and what will be the state of the world after the game. That’s why the scene that you asked about, we don’t want to be straightforward, but we are giving some suggestions that will probably reveal the state of the world in more comic books and other stuff. So there are discussions. There are discussions, but we are not setting one kind of ending.â

If held up to some scrutiny, the supposed V cameo is questionable. As some fans point out, the characterâs hairstyle isnât exactly the same as that of the âdefaultâ female V, and her cyberware isnât identical to that seen in 2077âs promo art, so even if the show were to be âcanonizingâ a specific version of V, this person doesnât look quite like the one you see on the gameâs box art. But ultimately, the show goes out of its way to not directly address Vâs fate, which can go in several directions depending on the playerâs choices.Â

âWhen we were creating Edgerunners [season one] and multiple comic books and board games, the canon was before the game, so we knew the state of the world.â he says. âAnd for the things post-game, it’s not that there are super-detailed canon things, but one important canon information is that Arasaka is weakened and that’s it. And it gives us a lot of opportunities to show the city in a different way.

But again, it’s not detailed. So it doesn’t make any of the endings canon. But the things that happened in the game could lead to that, whatever your choice was.â

I appreciate when creators for choice-driven franchises have this mindset, even if it means that future Cyberpunk projects canât incorporate characters who have multiple fates depending on the choices you make in 2077. Cyberpunk 2 is currently in development at CD Projekt Red. Weâll see if it sticks to this principle and allows for all potential endings of the first game whenever it comes out.

Helen Chiang, who became the Xbox division's first chief operating officer in July, says she has "serious concerns" about how her case was handled.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story."

Longtime Microsoft executive Helen Chiang was made Xbox's first-ever chief operating officer as part of the 'reset' in July, a role that gave her "end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services." Then, just three months later and with virtually no fanfare, she was gone, amidst an anonymous claim that she was "terminated for policy violations."

Saying it was important "to set the record straight," Chiang has now formally denied that claim in a lengthy LinkedIn post, saying she did not:

The record-straightening did not get into why Chiang did leave Xbox, although she seemed to imply that it was not an amicable departure: "I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they're applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously."

The sudden split seemed doubly strange because prior to taking the COO job at Xbox, Chiang spent more than 20 years at Microsoft, nearly all of it with the Xbox division—rising from Xbox platform business manager in 2007 to corporate vice president of the Minecraft franchise in 2020, a position she held for more than six years. The memo announcing Chiang's departure was also notably restrained: "Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today," Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote. "I'm grateful for her years of service and wish her well."

"I share this because I don't want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That's the legacy I hope to leave behind," Chiang wrote in her message.

"This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story."

I've reached out to Microsoft for comment on Chiang's message and will update if I receive a reply.

Rosario Dawson and Hayden Christensen know exactly how to get Star Wars fans worked up. Put them together, add a little Anakin-and-Ahsoka nostalgia, and people are already paying attention. Wrap both actors in sheer blue fabric so they look suspiciously like Force ghosts, and suddenly everyone starts wondering whether Dave Filoni is trying to tell us something about an upcoming movie release or another new Star Wars project. That is exactly what happened after Dawson shared a photo with Christensen that put a very funny spin on their Ahsoka connection.

In an Instagram post, the two Star Wars mainstays are not actually dressed as Ahsoka Tano and Anakin Skywalker. Christensen appears to be wearing regular clothes under a layer of translucent blue layer, while Dawson wears what looks more like a medieval or fantasy costume. If anything, the dress gives off a little Princess Fiona energy. See for yourself in her post below:

A post shared by rosariodawson (@rosariodawson)

Dawson made the joke even more obvious with her caption: “MAY THE FORCE GHOSTS BE WITH YOU 👻👻.”

The costumes are goofy, simple and immediately recognizable. Christensen looking like a Force ghost is also perfectly reasonable within Star Wars movie canon. Dawson getting the same treatment, however, is where fans started getting nervous. Because, uh… Why is Rosario Dawson a Force ghost?

To be clear, nobody at Lucasfilm announced the death of Ahsoka Tano's death through an Instagram costume photo. Dawson is not dressed as Ahsoka here, and there is no reason to think she casually spoiled one of the biggest possible developments in Ahsoka Season 2. That didn't stop fans from noticing the implication and asking a ton of questions.

Comments under the Clerks 2 actress's post quickly filled with people who remembered that becoming a Force ghost usually requires a fairly serious prerequisite. Fans wrote:

I understand the reaction. Ahsoka has survived Order 66, Darth Vader, the World Between Worlds and enough lightsaber fights to make most Jedi reconsider the profession entirely. She has also spent years bouncing between animated and live-action Star Wars, becoming one of the franchise's most durable characters in the process.

Christensen as a Jedi specter has precedent. Anakin appeared as a Force ghost at the end of Ahsoka Season 1, and the original trilogy was later reworked to insert the actor into the old footage. Christensen is also returning for Season 2, with Anakin expected to remain part of Tano's story.

Dawson's Ahsoka, meanwhile, is still very much alive when Season 2 begins. She and Sabine Wren remain stranded beyond the known galaxy while Grand Admiral Thrawn has returned home and prepares for whatever comes next. So when the actress playing her suddenly appears next to Anakin's actor, both covered in ghostly blue fabric, fans will read into it.

For now, though, I am choosing the much less stressful explanation. They found some blue fabric, put it over their heads, and somebody took a photo. Nobody is dying. Probably.

Season 2 of Ahsoka hits the streaming calendar on January 20, 2027, for everyone with a Disney+ subscription. Fans can also stream all of the Star Wars movies -- including the prequels featuring Hayden Christensen -- using that same membership.

#3680. There’s Footage Running Around That Might Be A First Look At A Persona 1 Remake

We now have an idea of what a Revelations: Persona remake could look like. There’s a video being passed around on the gaming leaks and rumors subreddit that purportedly contains footage of the first Persona game after it’s been hit with the Atlus remake-ification beam. It’s a short video, entirely in Japanese, that seems to depict a gaggle of teenagers trying to escape what looks like a haunted hospital.

As the main character (referred to as “boy with earring”) turns a corner, he’s attacked by a monster and the video cuts to a battle sequence. Surprisingly, it looks like the protagonist from Persona 2, Tatsuya Suou, makes an appearance in the battle, which also features a character who looks like Eriko Kirishima. Combat itself includes a highly stylized UI centered on the attacking character with options that include “persona,” “gun,” “sword,” “item,” and “defend,” as well as a turn order list and other info.

There’s no confirmation that this is real footage from a P1 remake and as of publication time, the Reddit thread and the page where the video link is hosted have not yet been subject to any takedown notices. There’s speculation this video could be a mod or a project that was vibe-coded with AI, but comments throughout the Reddit thread say that if it is fake, it’s incredibly well-done. Some commenters, however, are too busy arguingÂ  about whether or not it’s a good thing this “remake” looks reminiscent of Persona 5 and the remakes of Persona 3-4, and not more like the original Persona game its supposedly based on.

Earlier this year, Persona producer Wada Kazuhisa said in an interview that remaking the first entries in the series was something Atlus “should definitely do.” He noted that game development technology has advanced to the point where “we can now create new cutscenes that are more immersive and realistic than before,” which is certainly evident in…well, whatever that is.

#3679. Inside Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s Beloved 730-Acre Country Estate

On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge stables, her daughter, Zara Tindall, may be riding with her daughter and nieces, coaching them as they jump through courses designed by her father Mark Phillips. Meanwhile, Zara’s husband, rugby star Mike Tindall, may be playing beer pong in the “party barn” with his brother-in-law Peter Phillips, while Princess Anne’s husband Sir Timothy Laurence watches rugby in the cozy, cluttered parlor of the estate’s main Georgian mansion.

The scene is that of an idyllic country estate, a beloved family home that is also a working farm. It may also serve as an example to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle as they search for their own private estate in the British countryside. “Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work,” Princess Anne once said. “This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise I can’t stay here."

Since the ’70s, Gatcombe Park has been Princess Anne’s place of refuge from endless royal duties, a place to live the country life she loves. “Every year, month and day, I realise how fortunate and privileged I am to have grown up and spent most of my life in the countryside,” she told Country Life in 2020. “It’s not only the space, appreciating the seasons, the wildlife, the plant life, the arable crops and the livestock, but, most importantly, it’s the people who live and work there and understand the complexity of their environment.”

The estate was the perfect wedding present from the late Queen Elizabeth to her athletic, no-nonsense daughter and her first husband, Mark Phillips. The two Olympic equestrians first met at a party in 1968, although the meeting was not auspicious. “We had to be told that we’d met in 1968 before we remembered,” Anne recalled.

Zara Phillips riding her horse Toytown at Gatcombe Horse Trials, with Princess Anne and Tim Laurence, September 16, 2001.

They later reconnected and found they shared many things, including an obsession with nature, country life, and the world of elite equestrian competitions. “Anne couldn’t marry her horse, so she’s marrying Mark,” the then Prince Charles reportedly joked about his future brother-in-law. Princess Anne approached their upcoming wedding with the same stoicism she did everything. When asked if their relationship could withstand the pressure of publicity and public duties, the Princess was blunt. “Can? It’s got to, hasn’t it.”

The two were married on November 14, 1973, in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. From the start, Phillips, an active captain in 1st The Queen’s Dragoon Guards, proved to be cut from a different cloth. He refused all the Queen’s offers of titles and was not popular with some royals and their courtiers, with the protective Prince Charles reportedly nicknaming him “fog,” because he was “so thick, according to Kitty Kelley’s The Royals.” British journalist Auberon Waugh (the eldest son of novelist Evelyn Waugh) was even more brutal. He unkindly described him as “Princess Anne’s grinning, speechless husband, who, if you whistle at him, wets himself.”

The entrance hall with a stone floor and decorative pillars, June 1976.

In spite of naysayers, the couple forged ahead and began searching for the perfect country estate (“I’ve never been a city girl,” Anne noted). In 1976, former Home Secretary Lord Rab Butler, suggested the couple check out Gatcombe Estate, his family home outside of the village of Minchinhampton.

The estate featured over 700 acres of woods and cultivated farmland, stables, a fine herd of Hereford-Friesian cattle and a trout lake, “netting an income of between 14,000 and 18,000 pounds a year.” The five-bedroom neoclassical main house, built with Cotswold stone, was originally built in 1774. In 1820, the famous economist Davis Ricardo had the house redesigned. The exterior was covered in roses and wisteria, and the couple were instantly smitten. The interior was not as picturesque, with one friend describing it as “rather dreary, in some disrepair, with suspicions of dry rot.”

But the couple loved it. “We stood on the front steps and looked out at the view; it was quiet, it was secluded, it was peaceful with woods down each side of a long valley,” Phillips recalled. “I thought to myself—well, whatever is inside, we can change, given time. But this we can never change. This is just what we have been looking for.”

Peter Phillips, age 9, on horseback at Gatcombe Park, July 28, 1987.

A week later, Princess Anne took Queen Elizabeth to view the property. In June 1976, it was announced the Queen had purchased the home for the couple for a reported 500,000 to 750,000 pounds at the time. Workers on the estate suggested to reporters that Anne could help on a tractor. “Since the Princess can drive a tank, why not?” one quipped.

There was immediate backlash to the private purchase. “When members of the Labour Party government heard that the Queen was buying her daughter and son-in-law the farm and woodland property at such a price, left-wing members called for the introduction of a wealth tax,” the Australian Woman’s Weekly reported. “They pointed out that last year Parliament voted the royal family an extra $600,000 to help it pay its bills.”

MP Willie Hamilton took it a step further. “They’re gold-plated parasites. The lot of them. All parasites.”

For their part, the palace was tight-lipped, claiming the purchase was “an absolutely private matter.” Lord Butler also scoffed at the reported price, claiming it was not nearly as high.

Ignoring the noise, the couple began working to improve their new estate, insisting they would pay their own way. “People never believe me when I say that we’re just like any other young married couple with a mortgage,” Phillips said. Princess Anne did indeed drive a tractor, and Prince Andrew and Prince Edward were said to come down to help during harvest season. While his wife stayed at her apartment working in Buckingham Palace in London during the week, Phillips worked tirelessly on the farm, “so tired that I fell asleep in front of the television.”

Making good on their dream to turn Gatcombe into an A+ equestrian facility, the couple in 1983 hosted the inaugural Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing. The event became a mainstay on the elite equestrian calendar. Held every August, it featured Olympians competing in cross-county (courses often designed by Phillips), jumping and dressage events. Thousands attended the televised program each year, and many more visited at the annual craft fairs and the Gatcombe Food Festival.

Princess Anne with her bull terrier dogs at the British Horse Trials Championships, August 31, 1996.

Phillips found many ways to monetize the estate, even turning brushwood cleared from the courses into paintbrushes. Meanwhile, the couple raised their children Peter and Zara at Gatcombe, where life revolved around horses. “One enjoys riding, but when you get back there’s still half a day’s work to do just to keep the darn things on four legs,” Anne noted, per The Princess Royal by Helen Cathcart. “You have time for nothing else.”

Tindall has noted that she had an “amazing” country childhood on the estate, far from the hustle and bustle of royal life. “It was a great place to grow up around horses, looking after animals—the respect and partnership that you have to build with the animals, it teaches you so much you know growing up and as a kid,” she said.

But this didn’t mean that growing up on the farm wasn’t hard work. The Phillips children (whose parents declined for them to have titles) were expected to carry their weight. “We had to do everything with them,” Zara recalled. “We had to clean our tack. We had to muck them out.”

Zara, who eventually became an Olympic rider herself, recalled that her parents had very different ways of training. “Mum’s very relaxed. She’s like, Just, you know, just do what you do, whereas my father’s like, More of this, more of that, she said. “My father was quite critical... Very rarely you would get a, Yeah, that was good, out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment. He was a tough coach.”

There was also tension inside the home. Both Princess Anne and Phillips were unfaithful (Phillips even had a daughter, Felicity, with a New Zealand woman in 1985) and in 1989 they separated. But Phillips did not go far, moving to Aston Farm on the estate and continuing to run Gatcombe’s events (he finally left Aston Farm in 2013). Princess Anne stayed in the main house with her new husband, Sir Timothy Laurence, who she married in 1992.

According to those who have visited the main house, life there is surprisingly “unroyal” and laid-back, filled with bric-a-brac and cozy, worn decor. “Journalists and biographers who visit Gatcombe for the first time are still struck by the informality of the place,” Anne’s biographer Nicholas Courtney told Glocester Live. Gatcombe Park has become a true family compound, with Peter Phillips and his family reportedly having a cottage there. Zara and Mike Tindall have raised their children at Aston Farm since 2013.

Running the estate has also become a family affair. Peter Phillips helped organize the annual Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing in later years. Princess Anne would present trophies and Zara would compete, as photographers took pictures of Anne’s grandchildren frolicking.

Zara Phillips, Mia Tindall, and Princess Anne at the Whatley Manor Horse Trials, Gatcombe Park, September 8, 2017.

Farming operations have also continued, a practice Anne clearly relishes. “I have lived at Gatcombe for more than 42 years,” Anne wrote in Country Life in 2020. “We were not looking for a farm, but it has been a real privilege to try to work with what we have. Ours is an organic, extensive grass enterprise, usually complicated by running the horse-trial championships in early August. The woodland is a real mix of trees—mostly beeches, but huge numbers of ash of all ages. Who knows how many will survive, but I feel the naturally selected mix could be an important part of the answer.”

That same year, the official royal website also noted the extensive livestock on the property that included 230 Wiltshire Horn sheep, 14 White Park cows, 6 Highland cows, and 2 Gloucester Old Spot sows. There is also a prized herd of rare Suffolk Punch horses, which Anne is passionate about saving. The estate also includes a kitted out party barn, which includes catering facilities, large screens and bar/lounge areas.

The last few years have been eventful, in both good and bad ways. In 2021, Zara gave birth to her third child, Lucas, on the bathroom floor at Aston Farm. In 2023, the estate hosted their last Eventing Festival, citing rising costs and COVID as the reason.

“The horse trials at Gatcombe and more recently the Festival of British Eventing have been a major part of my life for over 40 years when The Princess Royal and I first had the dream,” Mark Phillips said in a statement at the time. “It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since COVID, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”

In 2024, Princess Anne was reportedly injured by a horse on the property, which resulted in her being hospitalized for a concussion. But there was happier news in June of 2026, when Peter Phillips and his new wife Harriet Sperling reportedly celebrated their wedding reception at the party barn.

Although Princess Anne still continues with her punishing schedule of official engagements, staying in her London apartment in St. James Palace when she must, it is clear her heart lies at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by her loved ones, beloved animals and the crisp country air. “It’s very normal; there isn’t any standing on ceremony, and she’s the only one with a title,” royal historian Robert Hardman told Hello!. “She’s a very good grandmother. She’s hands-on, but like all grandchildren, I think they can get away with things. She dotes on them.”

In fact, the normally tight-lipped Anne has said so herself. “It’s really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this.” Former royal courtier Ailsa Anderson agrees. “Gatcombe is her bolthole, where she is not the Princess Royal—she is Anne.”
