90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way's Andi Wallace and Nigel have me going back and forth on whether they'll stick together amidst issues navigating ethical non-monogamy. There were obvious red flags suggesting this couple wouldn't last until the end of the season. However, thanks to some recent updates, I'm not so sure now.

When I first learned about Andi being on Tinder, I assumed this was an open-and-shut case. Gone were the days of roaming supermarkets without shoes on. Now, I'm not sure what to think, and I'm eager to see the rest of this storyline play out on the 2026 TV schedule due to two new developments cropping up.

Halloween just came and went, and Andi had a pretty interesting choice for her costume. She went as Nigel, and mimicked a viral photo of him that's made rounds on the internet as of late. Take a look:

A post shared by Andi Jane (@andijanemusic)

Generally speaking, I don't think many people are in the habit of dressing up as their exes for Halloween. I've seen couples go as each other, or even as other couples. Is Andi dressing up like this because she wants to appease the 90 Day Fiancé fans, or is she paying tribute to her current fiancé? I'm not quite sure, because I'd wager most watching on TLC or with an HBO Max subscription wouldn't get this reference. However, that's just speculation on my part.

While Andi is dressing up like Nigel, the man himself is traveling across the world and hanging out with Azrael, the blue-haired woman recently introduced on 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way. Reddit has photos of them together chopping it up, dancing and kissing at some sort of music festival.

90 Day Fiancé's Shea Looks Almost Unrecognizable To Me After Weight Loss

Based on Andi's statements on feeling uncomfortable about Nigel and Azrael's relationship, I can't imagine she'd approve of that. In fact, she's been a bit alarmed by how many partners Nigel's had amid their time apart and has kept pushing for a monogamous relationship now that she's in Australia.

Given these recent developments, I can't tell if this means Andi has embraced the polyamorous lifestyle or not. It could be possible they're still together and that by the end of this season, she'll reveal she's made peace with him dating who he wants while she's away.

It's also possible Andi has simply decided this lifestyle isn't for her and harbors no ill feelings toward Nigel. He was, after all, pretty straight up about being polyamorous and said that asking him to stop that lifestyle was a deal-breaker. There's nothing wrong with Andi trying out a relationship to see if she can handle it, and ultimately realizing she wants someone who is exclusive to her.

Given all the uncertainty, I'm more eager than ever to see the latest episode of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way, which airs on TLC on Sundays at 8:00 p.m. ET. I have to wonder how anyone who has a successful polyamorous storyline feels about this, and if they're happy or mad about what they're seeing.

#3677. Undiscovered Star Wars Secret Finally Found, Dev Who Hid It: ‘It’s Been A Long 3 And A Half Years’

EAEaster EggStar WarsStar Wars Jedi: Survivor

Star Wars Jedi: Survivor was released back in 2023 and is a very good game with some fun Easter eggs and references hidden in it. But one secret remained hidden, even after the developer who included it in the third-person action game teased fans online about it. Now, someone has finally found the secret after inputting the Konami code in a menu.

Back in 2025, Respawn UI director Jordan DeVries posted cryptically on social media about a secret buried in Jedi: Survivor that players had yet to find. “Imagine shipping a (submitted, approved) UI easter egg in your game that no one has yet noticed or found,” posted the developer last year. That kicked off some players digging around the Soulslike Star Wars sequel for this hidden secret. But nobody seemingly found it until now, according to DeVries.

On November 1, DeVries shared on social media that user TowerBunga on Twitter had found the Easter egg after inputting the famous Konami code in the Force upgrade menu in Jedi: Survivor. And once entered correctly, a giant space frog appears and eats a strange moon in the sky. It’s a bizarre but amusing secret that took three years to find.

Kudos to the Jedi Survivor team on a *very* well hidden easter egg https://t.co/aB2Za99XKc pic.twitter.com/rWGa5ca3do

— Towerbunga ð SWCLA (@towerbunga) November 1, 2026

Over on Reddit, DeVries responded to the news that the well-hidden secret had been discovered. “It’s been a long three years…”

I always love when fans find secrets and Easter eggs in games many years after release. It’s a reminder that there are likely many, many secrets still buried in games, all of which are just waiting to be found by someone. It’s also a wonderful reminder that, despite it seeming like the internet has cataloged everything in every game, there still remains some mystery out there. Who knows? One day, you might stumble upon something nobody has seen before in an old game, and your discovery could end up as a blog on Kotaku dot com.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it? A high-fantasy survival crafting RPG set in the genre's most impressive sandbox. Release date: October 15, 2026 (1.0) Expect to pay: $40/£35 Developer: Keen Games Publisher: Keen Games Reviewed on: RTX 4080, AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 64GB RAM Steam Deck: Verified Link: Steam | Official site

High up on a mountain in the Albaneve Summits, just on the southern border of Enshrouded's new zone, I spot the perfect place for my next medieval building project. It seems safe with no nearby enemy spawns on the flat stretch of land, and there's even a cute frozen pond that gives it real Christmas-card appeal. I love it, and I'll love it even more once I've built a cliffside castle.

The only problem is I can't find a way up by climbing or gliding, so I'll have to make my own. I could build something, but that takes time, and I'm impatient. Instead, I behave like an absolute heathen—I bomb and pickaxe the hell out of the mountainside, carving a tunnel from the base to the top. It doesn't look great, but that's a problem for tomorrow's Flameborn.

That's always been one of my favorite parts of Enshrouded: you can destroy or build practically anything, anywhere in Embervale's voxel-based world. It's a survival crafting sandbox filled to the brim with handcrafted details, and every location still hidden by the fog of war could hold a new material, powerful weapon, or scenic vista. There's nothing quite like it, and just like the updates before, Enshrouded's 1.0 build keeps finding new, inventive ways to impress me long after I thought its well of surprises had run dry.

Enshrouded is a weird one. Not quite a traditional survival crafting game, but not a typical action RPG either. Its combat system and base building options are far more robust than most of its survival crafting cousins, but it's not nearly as brutal. I'm driven less by desperation and more by a desire to explore Embervale—a land devastated by a mysterious, malignant miasma known as (you guessed it) the Shroud. There's hardly a soul left in the world, so you learn more about its history from journals. Some are hastily scribbled by would-be heroes like you, while others are tragic retellings of someone's final days.

A few survivors remain as recruitable NPCs for your base. I love how lively they make player-made homes feel, even if the AI is a bit dopey.

One of my favorite additions in 1.0 is the voiceover added to every journal. The same narrator reads them all, giving the whole thing an endearing storybook feel as he shifts tone and pitch for different authors.

I found my favorite journal in a tiny, mountainside cave left by an old man grieving his wife. You can wander around the surrounding area for more environmental storytelling, but I have to warn you: some details got me teary-eyed.

So, for what must be the millionth time in my career, I stumble out of a mystical, sleepy haze confused and poorly dressed for the world I've awakened to. I am the Flameborn—a sort of ordained-by-god chosen one and the last hope for restoring the ruins of Embervale—but for now, I certainly don't feel that way. I just feel like some guy. It's a title I'll have to grow into, but will have to wait until I've upgraded from the aptly named 'ragged armor set'. Yeesh.

Enshrouded follows most of those rags-to-riches genre basics, so of course I'll graduate from an era of fighting with sticks and eating fistfuls of berries to magic-infused swords and Michelin-star meals. I've played so many of these games that the flow comes naturally now, but what I like most about Enshrouded's take on classic survival systems is that it drops the more punitive elements like fatigue, crafting chance, and even structural integrity.

Enshrouded has a robust set of custom difficulty options, but I learned the hard way to leave them alone until after you've tried the first dungeon.

An early access update added a custom setting for dehydration and starvation, but I much prefer playing without it .

There's cooking, farming, and even animal husbandry. Those systems are compelling enough as is, and don't gain anything by adding do-this-or-die mechanics.

Enshrouded knows that I, much like the family Golden Retriever, am treat-motivated. As long as there's shelter, fire, and decor, I'll get a stamina-boosting buff just by hanging out at home, but I'll never die from lack of sleep. In that regard, it's more like Valheim. Unique furnishings have their own comfort stats too, so there's incentive to explore Embervale for a new rug, fireplace, or even a toilet if you want a longer, more powerful boost. It's an especially exciting system for players like me, someone who loves building and decorating bases, but rarely sees a reward for the extra effort.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All this meticulous decorating makes me wonder whether I really want Enshrouded to add enemy raids on player bases and risk destroying them, but I'm leaning toward yes. It's the one major survival mechanic I miss in its formula, and I can't help but wistfully remember how fun it is to scramble into action when Valheim warns, "The forest is moving..." Imagine that, but with Enshrouded's poisonous fog instead.

Enshrouded has always been my favorite survival-crafting block set, but I'm thrilled with the new build camera. Building in tight corners is less hassle, and I don't slide off the roof a dozen times..

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd. It's nice to go from picking at scraps to being overwhelmed by choice

Version 1.0 also added Sparkworks, a logic system for creating your own enemy spawns, player-triggered events, special world builds, custom dungeons, and more. Your creations are shareable, too, so other players can suffer through your cruel obstacle course designs. I've tinkered with it myself, but I've mostly spent my time exploring player-made hobbit holes and feeling painfully self-conscious by comparison.

Repetitive tasks—another hunt for a rare material, another trek across the map—can become exasperating even in the best survival crafting games. There's a thin line between tedium and satisfaction, and Enshrouded walks it better than most. Much of that is thanks to the game's philosophy around punishment and reward, but its RPG elements add a layer of complexity that more than makes up for anything missing from Enshrouded's "survival-lite" approach.

Take my group, for example. I play with seven other friends, while that feels like a lot for most survival crafting games, Enshrouded's combat roles give us distinctly useful jobs. Rather than dumping points into three or four barebones stats, your Flameborn can specialize across 12 different skill trees. I mostly opt for tank, athlete, and assassin perks, but my allies fill other needs with mix-and-match builds for glass-cannon wizards, battlemage healers, or stealthy assassins. We also have our preferred responsibilities, like mining, woodcutting, gardening, cooking, and all those other usual genre chores.

Enshrouded's boss fights are a blast and more dynamic than similar games. Fights aren't as mechanically heavy as a Conan Exiles dungeon boss, but the traditional tank-and-spank approach won't cut it.

Hollow Halls—Enshrouded's massive dungeons that practically demand group play—are where combat roles shine the most. I beat one playing solo, but also wiped several times in a group of four.

A word of caution: multiplayer groups of more than two or three people should consider a dedicated server. Version 1.0 significantly improves performance, but not enough to spare bigger parties from the occasional murderous lag spike.

Multiplayer is also where some of my biggest gripes with Enshrouded remain, and despite heavy reworks to its questing systems, my group still struggled to make sense of the journal when our objectives fell out of sync. Our confusion mostly stemmed from completing world progression quests without the full party, so when absent friends logged back in, their to-do list didn't look the same and they had a list of missed quests. There are separate, personal quests to do at your own leisure, but we constantly compared our journals to make sure no one had gone off course.

I'm still not sure if any of that even mattered. No one was ever locked out of crafting recipes or new biomes because of the discrepancies, so the punishment boiled down to a smidge of missed XP and simply missing out on the moment. It didn't end up being a big deal, and I'm starting to think the journal's 'missed quest' label made the whole thing feel more consequential than it actually was. I clenched my jaw in frustration a few times, but if that's my biggest nitpick, then Enshrouded is survival crafting gold.

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd.

As much as I love the genre, I can't pretend it isn't filled with seemingly eternal early access pits. I've played in plenty of messy sandboxes, a handful of good ones, and just a few great ones. Then there's Enshrouded, operating in a league of its own. But even then, Enshrouded isn't just a good survival crafting game: it's a damn good game by any measure. Its building tools reward even my most impractical ambitions, and I'll never grow tired of exploring Embervale's hidden nooks and crannies.

Few games in the genre match its distinct identity or degree of polish, and after 500+ hours of adventuring, there's little left to wish for. My biggest dilemma post-Enshrouded will be moving on from a survival crafting RPG so lovingly handcrafted. I fear Keen Games has cooked up something that has forever changed my palate.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

Andrea has been covering games for nearly a decade, picking up bylines at IGN, USA Today, Fanbyte, and Destructoid before joining the PC Gamer team in 2025. She's got a soft spot for older RPGs and is willing to try just about anything with a lovey-dovey "I can fix them" romance element. Her weekly to-do always includes a bit of MMO time, endlessly achievement hunting and raiding in Final Fantasy 14. Outside of those staples, she's often got a few survival-crafting games on rotation and loves a good scare in co-op horror games.

#3675. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Ballhog'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's zeitgeist snapshot explains what ballhog means, how a video of someone wrapping a burger led to a new meme format, and the dangers of Benny tripping. So strap in, and let's go.

Ballhog or ball hog is a streetwear fashion style growing in popularity among younger people. The cool ones, anyway. The idea is to wear vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique. Like the best youth trends, it's an insider vs. outsider thing that takes connoisseurship to understand. Some examples: If you're wearing a late 1990s Helmut Lang denim jacket, most people will think "thrifted," but a ballhog-enjoyer would recognize it as a seminal piece of streetwear history. If you want to be ballhog, rocking a pair of skinny jeans isn't going to cut it unless they're from Dior Homme or at least Cheap Monday.

The style is named after the Ball Hog Collective, a group of rappers, Twitch streamers, and content creators founded by the Atlanta-based indie record label Ballhog. It was popularized by streamer Brady Goodwin, seen below looking quite ballhog:

The #ballhog hashtag is blowing up (as people used to say) lately with a growing collection of kids posting videos to show off their ballhog fits, like so:

The popularity of the style comes down to, I think, how difficult it is to commodify. Most truly organic trends are recognized quickly by culture vulture types, and in a few months, there's a line of clothes at Target, but you can't do that with ballhog. There's no way to make "new" ballhog gear, as that would mark it as inauthentic immediately. Gotta hand it to the kids for adopting a style that is at once exclusionary and impossible to rip off.

On the opposite edge of the spectrum from ballhog fashion is the "while they're out partying btw" meme, videos made to show off the strange, specific, and usually useless talent one develops while others are out wearing cool clothes and socializing. The phrase has been kicking around since last year, when TikToker @tacobella posted this video

but it's taken off more recently, thanks to the huge number of views on this video showing off some truly mind-blowing burger wrapping skills:

This led to an influx of videos of people showing off what they were doing instead of partying. Like this mechanic:

This is the second youth trend I support wholeheartedly. We can't all be cool ballhoggers and we don't all have talent, but we can all learn to do a thing really well through brute force and repetition.

The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

As for "scuba," it now describes something that is very smelly, which might be because the word conjures the dead air of unventilated, underwater spaces. But it's often accompanied by a pinch-your-nose gesture, which looks like the gesture in the Scuba Dance that was popular on TikTok a few months ago, so that's a more likely origin for the term.

There has been a steady stream of news stories about kids overdosing on Benadryl over the last few years. They call it "Benny tripping," and it's achieved by taking too much of the allergy medicine, like 10 times the amount recommended. Among the active ingredients in Benadryl is Diphenhydramine, and it's a particularly nasty drug. Unlike most recreational substances, tripping on Benadryl is not fun. It's a deliriant, and taking too much results in hallucinations that are usually described as terrifying—swarms of spiders, shadow people, whispering voices, etc. Benadryl overdoses can result in loss of short term memory, displacement from time and space, and panic attacks that last for hours or even days. Or you die from tachycardia. Here's how Reddit user Reasonable-County971 described their experience,

I lost access to my memories. I couldn’t recognize my mom—I mistook her for a 'pretty nurse'. Early in the trip, before you lose yourself, you develop tremendous anxiety, far far beyond anything else I can compare it to. Also, you have motor skills affected, including losing access to your bladder.

So yeah, it's a bad drug. And it's easy to get—just pop down to CVS. On the plus side, despite sometimes overly hysterical reporting on Benadryl as an "online trend" or challenge, tripping on Benadryl is such a harrowing, not-at-all-fun experience, its use isn't particularly popular among young people. But if you want to scare yourself, read some trip reports, watch this YouTube video, and imagine someone you love going through this.

This week's viral video is very meta, and it's hilarious to anyone who follows the trajectory of viral internet sensations. Brought to us by the great @ariisaysso, this video lays out the history of the fictional Cheezit Girl as she becomes an internet sensation, quits her job, sells merch, releases a rap single, releases a remix, reheats the nachos, and falls into obscurity, all in about two and a half minutes. We've seen this story before with the Hawk Tuah Girl, Dah Bih Gah Kid, and many more future members of the "remember that thing" club, and we'll no doubt see it all again soon. Such is the circle of life.

#3674. A 21-Year Veteran Of Xbox Who Is Suddenly No Longer At The Company Says She Has ‘Serious Concerns’ About The Whole Process

Helen Chiang had been at Microsoft since 2005. She spent over a decade overseeing Minecraft, the company’s most important gaming franchise, and survived this year’s big Xbox “reset” with a promotion to the role of the gaming division’s chief operating officer. Barely three months later, she’s suddenly out at the company she called home for more than two decades, a development which generated tons of speculation about whether she was fired or not. Chiang now says she’s breaking her silence to set the record straight.

“There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was ‘fired for a policy violation,'” she wrote on LinkedIn, referencing a report last month from Eurogamer alleging she was fired for a “policy violation.” “Thatâs not accurate and while I wonât turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. Itâs important to me to set the record straight.”

Chiang went on to say that she never leaked confidential company information to the press or went outside of company-authorized communication channels. She said she also did not leave the company for a competitor, nor did she “engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Chiang added that her past results and record speak for themselves, and that she did not leave the company because she’d been passed over for a bigger role. The chief operating officer role had not been something she’d lobbied for.

“I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others,” she wrote. “Those standards only mean something when theyâre applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I donât want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. Thatâs the legacy I hope to leave behind.”

“We donât discuss individual personnel matters,” a spokesperson for Microsoft previously told Kotaku regarding Chiang’s departure. “Weâre grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

The sudden move comes amid a massive reorganization of Xbox that has seen massive layoffs and studio divestitures as Microsoft seeks to rebuild the platform while also improving its bottom line. As chief operating officer, Chiang would have had a central role in helping to restructure and better optimize the tech giant’s gaming business ahead of the next console generation, Project Helix, which is reportedly set to arrive in 2028. Though the Xbox veteran set out to clear the air amid much of the recent speculation about her departure from the company, it’s still not clear what exactly happened.

“For the first time, we are establishing a Chief Operating Officer with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote back in July. “Helen Chiang has been promoted to this role and will report directly to me. Over nearly two decades at XBOX, Helen has helped build some of our most important businesses, from XBOX Live to leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise. She will bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Sharma later told The Wall Street Journal “clarity is kindness” when describing the tough choices she was making to set the stage for an ambitious future. “Clarity is Kindness” is also how Chiang began her LinkedIn post today. âThis is not how I ever imagined my story here would end,” she wrote. “And it is not the whole story.â

#3673. Little Shop of Horrors: An Oral History

Like an unassuming plant from outer space, Little Shop of Horrors had humble beginnings—but managed to blossom at a surprising rate. The musical is performed numerous times each year across the globe; the current Off Broadway production has been running for seven years straight. But none of that would have happened without the 1986 film version of Little Shop, a cult classic that Warner Bros. executives once characterized as “the highest-budget musical they’d ever done,” according to its director, Frank Oz. “I don’t know if it’s true or if it’s hyperbole, but that’s what they told me to pressure me into doing a good job.”

“I love it. Audiences love it,” says composer Alan Menken. “Anytime I watch Little Shop,” though, “every other second I’ll be thinking about my late collaborator”—lyricist, book writer, and original stage director Howard Ashman, whom he worked with on both the original stage show and the film. “I’ll look at his work and how amazing it is,” Menken says. “Then people come running up to me, and I go, ‘It’s Howard.’”

Moranis as Seymour Krelborn and Ellen Greene as Audrey in Frank Oz's 1986 film adaptation.

It’s been nearly 40 years since Audrey II began its cinematic rampage. To commemorate the movie—which is getting a brand-new 4K restoration and rerelease on Blu-ray—Vanity Fair spoke with Oz, Menken, producer David Geffen, stars Rick Moranis, Ellen Greene, Tisha Campbell, Tichina Arnold, Michelle Weeks, and more about assembling an A-list cast including Steve Martin and Bill Murray; the film’s long, difficult production; why Moranis had to film several of his scenes as though he was moving in slow motion; and the movie’s elaborate, expensive, utterly depressing original ending.

Back in 1959, legendary low-budget filmmaker Roger Corman had a challenge: to shoot an entire film in two days. He enlisted Charles B. Griffith to write a film using preexisting sets—including a florist shop and a dental office. The original Little Shop of Horrors was born: a scrappy but ambitious B movie featuring a brief cameo by a young Jack Nicholson.

The film became a staple of late-night television, entrancing viewers like a teenage Howard Ashman. As an adult, Ashman knew it’d make a great musical. His agent watched the Corman film and told Ashman he was out of his mind.

Poster for the TV adaptation of The Little Shop of Horrors, 1960.

Ashman then approached jingle writer Alan Menken about doing the musical with him at the WPA Theatre, of which Ashman was a cofounder.

ALAN MENKEN (COMPOSER): I thought it was absolutely amazing. This was one of those so-bad-it’s-good movies. When we first took a crack [at writing the songs], it was actually very close to the Corman film…. And then Howard said, “You know, I think we should do this as the dark side of Grease.”

You think about those beach blanket horror movies from the early ’60s or late ’50s, and there is both a tackiness and an incredible exuberance about them at the same time. And then you think about the Phil Spector Wall of Sound and his work with the Ronettes. So the score became a whole homage to all those early rock influences, and it just became a perfect tonal bed for the storytelling.

ELLEN GREENE (“AUDREY,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY AND THE 1986 FILM): I got to watch Howard direct several sessions with Alan playing on the piano. They counterbalanced each other; Howard was very serious, and Alan is just a sweetheart. Although Howard was also a sweetheart.

MENKEN: What makes for a good collaboration, first of all, is to get your fucking egos out of the room. Bring your talent into the room and always be ready to throw something out…. Don’t ever allow yourself to fall in love with your own work. You are driving this particular thing called a musical. Howard was the best I ever experienced at doing that…. Howard knew exactly what he wanted.

GREENE: I remember walking down the street [listening to a demo of the song “Skid Row” and thinking], I don’t want to do a camp musical. [Then I] got too unemployed, and I'm listening to “Somewhere That’s Green.” I started quietly singing “Green” to myself, and it made me cry. And I knew right then and there I had an Audrey inside of me that was waiting to be born…. When I went into the audition, I did the scenes, and the speaking voice just came out of me.

Michelle Weeks, Tisha Campbell, and Tichina Arnold as Chiffon, Crystal, and Ronette, respectively, in the 1986 adaptation.

LEE WILKOF (“SEYMOUR,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY): I got a call from a casting director that I knew in New York. [She said], “A theater in New York is doing a musical based on the movie Little Shop of Horrors…. Would you come in and read for the part of the dentist? I walked into the audition…and Howard Ashman looked at me and he went, “You’re not a dentist. Would you mind going out and looking at the role of Seymour?” And I did, and I got a callback. Apparently, it was between me and another actor. His name’s Nathan Lane. And the assistant director apparently said that she thought that I would work better as a Seymour. Her name’s Connie Grappo, and we’ve been married 42 years.

GREENE: I was a brunette at the time. I said, “Howie, meet me at 14th Street.”… And I tried on a long blonde wig with bangs, and he went, “I don’t know what you’re doing.” I said, “Just let me finish.” Paul Holmes, the stage manager, helped me cut the wig, and Howard still wasn’t sure. Then I completed the look [with a black cocktail dress], and he loved it.

The show opened at the WPA in 1982 for what was supposed to be a two-week “showcase,” with the actors all making a mere $50 a week in exchange for being reviewed by major theater critics. It was an immediate success.

WILKOF: It was impossible to get a ticket. It went from being this obscure little show. The word on the street apparently grew.

MENKEN: We had lines of producers around the block.

DAVID GEFFEN (PRODUCER): I don’t quite remember how I first got involved, but I think Cameron Mackintosh and I were approached…. I thought it was terrific.

Director of photography Robert Paynter on set, 1986.

MENKEN: We knew there were people who wanted to bring Little Shop to Broadway, and Howard said absolutely not.

GEFFEN: The [Off Broadway] show was very successful, highly thought of. Then we opened it up in Los Angeles. It was natural that we’d make it as a movie.

The creative team began planning a feature film, which Geffen would produce. Tom Cruise, per Menken, wanted to play Seymour (although his reps have claimed he wasn’t interested in the role); he was immediately vetoed by Ashman. Geffen had his eyes set instead on a comedic actor from Canada.

RICK MORANIS (“SEYMOUR”): I first started hearing about the film being made early on, like ’82 or ’83. I ran into David Geffen randomly—I had never met him before—and he stopped me and said, “I want you in my movie.” I said, “Which one?” And he told me, and I said, “Well, okay!” And then for the next three years, I would occasionally hear about it or read about it in the hands of one director or another, and nothing ever happened.

At one point, Steven Spielberg was slated to produce the film, with Martin Scorsese directing. John Landis was also attached to the project for a time. Perhaps the name that made the most sense on paper was Frank Oz, best known as the man who brought to life childhood staples like Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, and Yoda.

FRANK OZ (DIRECTOR): I saw [the show] and thought it was amazing. But I didn’t have a take on it. And when I read the script for the movie, I couldn’t get my hands around it. It was so big, and I didn’t have a clear vision of it. So, through my agents, I said, “Thank you, but I can’t do it.” Two weeks later, something clicked in me regarding the three girl-group singers. I realized that when they entered onstage, all they could do was enter from the left or from the right…. But in a movie, it’s 360 degrees; you can have them enter from anywhere. So that’s what kind of changed my idea. I called back and I said, “You know, I may have a way to do this,” and then David asked me to do a rewrite…. Then I went to London, and I spent a month on the rewrite, and I felt really good about it. I knew if I said yes [to directing it], that’d mean two years of my life would be on this project. But I was committed and excited about it.

GREENE: [Frank] has to see the vision. Until he sees the vision in his mind’s eye, in his head, he will not take something on.

Greene, Steve Martin as Orin Scrivello, and Moranis, 1986.

MORANIS: [It’s] the intersection of so many skills and qualities that he has: a remarkable sense of humor, a real affinity for the darker arts and all the puppeteering, and such a keen eye for design.

OZ: I had not known Rick, who is now one of my closest friends after all these years. I never knew Rick, never heard of him because I was in London shooting for five years, and Rick was doing SCTV, and that was not shown in London. But I saw some of his work and I thought it was brilliant.

MORANIS: I knew this was an extraordinary opportunity to do a musical, and shoot it in London, and work with Frank and that cast. [Film] musicals don’t come along too often for people who get to call themselves actors.

OZ: David understandably wanted a star, but…I couldn’t see an Audrey with the depth and the heart that was given to the character by Ellen. I couldn’t see that being done by anyone else. So I asked him to please let me do a screen test with Ellen, and he did. And that’s when David said yes to Ellen.

MORANIS: Ellen had created the character of Audrey for the Off Broadway show many years before we did the movie.  She wasn’t just acting the part of Audrey; she was Audrey. I had just come from years of comedic character acting on SCTV and in films like Strange Brew and Ghostbusters. So we were both approaching our performances for Little Shop in similar ways. I think that’s why we had such a strong onscreen chemistry.

GREENE: Frank saw the character a little more heroine-like [than she was onstage]. He wasn’t sure about the “Audrey-isms,” and so that’s why the line “You don’t meet nice boys when you live on Skid Row, Mr. Mushnik” is not in the film…. Freddy Cooper was a cameraman…and he’s the reason I got to do the squeak in the film. Frank and Rick weren’t sure, and he spoke up and said, “Sir, I think it’s funny.”

OZ: David also suggested Steve Martin, and Steve I had worked with a little bit prior to that. Steve and I talked, and at the time there was a very popular character called Fonzie, and Steve said he just didn’t want to do Fonzie. I said, “Absolutely, that’s fine.” He wanted it more like Elvis. I said, “Fantastic.” As far as I was concerned, Steve could do anything.

The film’s glue wasn’t any of its big names; it was the three girls, all under 18, who made up its ’60s-girl-group-esque Greek chorus.

TISHA CAMPBELL (“CHIFFON”): I had just auditioned to play Regina King’s best friend in 227, and I didn’t get it. So I quit. I was 16 years old. I wanted to go to camp with my friends. And while I was there, my mother called me. She said, “Your agent keeps bugging me. They won’t stop calling me.” I said, “Did you tell them I quit?” And she said, “I told them and said you just wanted to be a regular kid, and they were like, ‘Please, just this one audition. Then you can go to camp.’ Can you just do it and I’ll send you right back to camp? No harm, no foul.” And I was like, “Okay, fine.”

MICHELLE WEEKS (“RONETTE”): At the time, I was on Broadway doing Tap Dance Kid, and I had a management company submit me. When I went for the audition…I was like, Yeah, they’re not gonna pick me. I’m too big. But then when we went for the callbacks, I was like, Oh, I have a chance!

Steve Ross, Courtney Sale, Steven Spielberg, and David Geffen at an off-Broadway performance of Little Shop of Horrors, 1982.

TICHINA ARNOLD (“CRYSTAL”): [I was] starting off in the theater [as] a little kid with wide eyes and ready to get it cracking. I just so happened to know Michelle Weeks because she and I went to school together. We had the same friends, and then Tisha and I knew each other from just auditioning.

CAMPBELL: They auditioned girls from everywhere…. And it just so happened that [the three girls cast were] from the tristate area. Michelle was from Brooklyn, Tichina was from Queens, and I was from New Jersey.

ARNOLD: And Frank Oz, we asked him, “How did you choose us?” And he was just like, “You girls had a synergy.”

Little Shop presented a real technical challenge: how to capture chemistry between its lead, Rick Moranis, and the man-eating plant. For the voice of the plant—named Audrey II by Seymour—the creative team turned to Motown singer Levi Stubbs. But actually bringing the creature to life would be the real struggle.

OZ: There’s only two words necessary, and that’s [puppeteer] Lyle Conway. Lyle passed recently, sadly, but Lyle is the one responsible for the plant. He was a pure artist, and he did an incredible job.

BRIAN HENSON (PRINCIPAL PUPPETEER): I think [Lyle] brought almost everybody that was on Return to Oz, and then a lot more because it was a much bigger build…. My dad [Jim Henson] came and visited the shoot a couple times, for sure. And then my little sister, Heather, was in it. She’s in the dentist scene.

BRAN FERREN (SPECIAL VISUAL EFFECTS): Lyle Conway was brilliant, his vision for how to create—because there wasn’t one plant; there were a series of plants that were used to show its various stages of growth.

OZ: I needed pure lip sync, really good lip sync, not just a mouth opening and closing. Because you’re on film, they can see in a tight shot that it’s just a puppet if it’s just opening and closing.

HENSON: This was definitely the biggest and the most complex [thing] that had ever been done in animatronics. It was also before the Creature Shop–type people were using motors, so it was almost all cable-driven.

OZ: All the performers had to rehearse the song over and over and over to make sure they hit every single syllable.

HENSON: There’s no eyes on that character, so it was always going to be the physical presence of the plant combined with this mouth and this voice. So Levi’s recordings were very important to Frank. [But] we started rehearsing before he even had Levi’s recordings.

MORANIS: They were looking for ways to make vowels and consonants so that they could form words, and then form phrases, and then be able to do that to music. And it was only possible to do at a slower motion than 24 frames a second.

There are 24 still frames in every second of standard film. But during rehearsals, it was discovered that the plant could not believably lip-synch at that speed. The production’s solution was to slow down Audrey II’s motions—operating the plant at 12 frames per second, then speeding the film up later so that it would look normal. This meant that anytime Moranis was in the same shot as the plant, he also had to move, act, and sing in slow motion.

MORANIS: The trick was to keep my butt tight. Because we keep our butt tight when we’re walking quickly. And when you try and walk slowly, it’s very easy to let your butt relax. If you were to look at that at 24 frames, you would look like you were doing some sort of weird walk. So by keeping the butt tight, I managed to pull it off, I think.

GREENE: [Frank] taught me how to act at 12 frames per second. He put me in a room; he had a camera. He said, “Ellen, walk across the floor.” He set it up to the regular speed. He said, “Now look at this,” and it looked like I was rocking back and forth. He showed me how you have to walk only forward, and ballet sort of helped. I worked on acting, talking, and moving in 12 frames a second.

John Candy as Wink Wilkinson and Moranis as Seymour Krelborn, 1986.

FERREN: How do you put emotion into a plant? I mean, news flash: It wasn’t a real man-eating plant! And my suspicion is that not many people watching the movie said, “Oh my God, they found an actual man-eating plant.” If you get it right, they shouldn’t be thinking about that.

HENSON: When we started rehearsing, we just had a bit of skin for the lips. The head was bald, and it was quite lightweight. Every week they’d build a little bit more, and it would just get heavier and heavier and heavier. By the end, it weighed more than 150 pounds.

With the cast—and plant—in place, filming began on October 21, 1985, at Pinewood Studios on the 007 Stage. Per Frank Oz’s vision, it had to be done entirely on a soundstage, as the world they were creating couldn’t come to life on location.

OZ: Roy Walker, our brilliant production designer, and I walked through the whole set. I told him where I felt things needed to be for each particular number, because I had planned the numbers in my head months before I even got to London.

GREENE: [As] someone who first was on this tiny, tiny stage, [I walked] into Pinewood Studios…and there in front of me is the land that is built, that I only saw in my mind's eye because I was on the stage—and it’s even better than I ever imagined.

OZ: My goal was to make it a movie sensibility instead of only a theatrical sensibility. It’s really a mixture of it, and my real goal was to make sure it reflected the gritty atmosphere of an Off Broadway play, and not a musical. I didn’t want to make it into Hello, Dolly! or Mame.

MENKEN: Little Shop is meant to be this tacky show in a hole-in-the-wall…and they wanted the film to have that same quality.

OZ: The opening number is packed with information. You have the three girls dancing in the streets. I needed people to know that they were not regular human beings, so I had them sing in the rain—and they were not affected by the rain.

ARNOLD: Frank Oz explained to us, “It’s gonna be raining around you, but you won’t get wet.” And I was like, “How is that gonna happen?” He showed us the pipes and stuff that they had in the ceiling and said, “Okay, so choreography-wise, you’re gonna follow this path [to ensure you don’t get wet].”

CAMPBELL: Man, it was raining on our heads! The first time we filmed that scene, it was raining so hard that you could tell on our faces. They had to cut. They were like, “You can’t show that it’s raining on y’all!”

WEEKS: We had to be up early in the morning, and us being teenagers, we were going places we weren’t supposed to go, like the club. We used to go to the Hippodrome and get out at like two or three in the morning, and have to be at the studio at six. But it was so much fun!

OZ: I loved shooting “Suddenly Seymour.” When Roy showed me the set—which is beautiful—I saw that staircase that he made. I thought, Okay, it’s got to be a Romeo-and-Juliet section where she’s up there, and he’s down there, and he runs up there. So it was all built up to that moment. I had him run up the stairs 30 to 40 times.

GREENE: Fifty-three takes we had to go up those stairs. [The “Suddenly Seymour”] set was so beautiful, with grass growing through the cracks and bricks and cobblestones. If any set was ever called a work of art, I think this would be applicable.

CAMPBELL: [Steve Martin] was very quiet off camera. But when that camera rolled, I was just in awe of how he would light up and become this character, and just be very big and broad.

OZ: When David suggested Billy [Murray, who has a cameo in the dentist scene]—and I knew Billy before that—I called him. I said, “Hey, Billy, do you want to do this?” And Bill said, “Do I have to do the words?” And I said, “No. I don’t care what words you use as long as you’re the masochist and he’s the sadist. That’s all I care about.”

As technical as the film itself was, nothing could compare to the plant.

OZ: People tend to think, Oh, puppets, that’s no problem. They are the hardest things in the world to shoot, to do right…. Just “Feed Me” alone took five weeks to shoot.

HENSON: Nowadays, you think of a film unit shooting 30 to 40 setups a day. Little Shop of Horrors was way down at three to five, five to seven if you were shooting easier stuff. It was slow, meticulous shooting. And Frank is a very meticulous director.

OZ: We’d usually go about 25 to 30 takes to make it perfect.

MORANIS: [For] “Feed Me,” Brian was inside the head of the plant, and then all the other puppeteers were connected to the plant. The actual plant store that we shot in was constructed on the second floor, and the first floor is where the puppeteers set up camp and where their cables would go down to. They would have monitors, and they could watch themselves operate the plant.

HENSON: There were vines that were being worked by one or two people on each vine. It [took] maybe five of us to work the head…. With “Mean Green Mother”…there’d be puppeteers all the way around the outside of the set, doing cables, and on the roof of the set was another maybe 10 puppeteers. And the set was also on top of a tank, so they could get to the underside of the pot for the roots.

MORANIS: It was so enjoyable to do [“Feed Me”]. I don’t think I had a moment when I didn’t enjoy shooting it. I do remember one aspect, just because it went on for so long: Every day I would come in and put on the same clothes.[Just] put on the same clothes every day for five weeks, or whatever it was.

HENSON: [During “Feed Me”], I’m right there. I said to Lyle, “You know, I just can’t stay hidden all the time.”… I couldn’t hide completely behind the stem. And Lyle said, “Okay, this is what we’re going to do. You’re going to wear a skintight green Lycra suit, and I’m gonna glue leaves to it.” There’s bits of me in the shots, but you don’t know it’s me.

The stage version of Little Shop ends with the plant eating Audrey, Seymour, and, finally, the audience. The filmmakers were determined to capture that same spirit, and did so in a $5 million epic ending that saw Audrey II taking over New York—ending on top of the Statue of Liberty.

OZ: Before I even went to London, I was at David Geffen’s office, and David said to us, “You know, you can’t end it the way the play ends it, because you’re killing your leads.” And Howard and I both said, “Well, we want to be true to the ending from Off Broadway, in part because we just like being true to things, but also because it was a deal with the devil. He deserved to die because he killed people, even though he didn’t do it maliciously.”

GREENE: I gravitate to the dark underpinnings of the Faustian tale. Even though there's a magical world full of whimsy and silliness and goofiness, it has a moral with dark underpinnings.

OZ: Richard Conway had worked about nine months on the models of the destruction at the end. It was no CGI, no opticals. Richard had built all this stuff, and then built the small plant that would be on the bridge, and he did an incredible job having the plants like Godzilla raging through the city.

MORANIS: I remember that, when I saw the ending of the play, something was off with it, but it didn’t matter because the vines came out of the ceiling. And I thought, This is brilliant! They’re distracting you from the tragic ending by creating this fun experience of stuff flying out of the ceiling.You’re part of the action. The shock and surprise, and all the tactile fuzziness of it, distracted from whatever was lacking in a fulfilling happy ending. It didn’t occur to me that that would become a problem in the film.

This is Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors, 1986.

GREENE: In the play, I say a line—“When I die, which should be very shortly…”—just to lighten the moment, and it’s silly. It releases some of the energy in the audience. But when I say it in the film, it’s very intimate, and it’s to Seymour. It’s weighted differently…. I’m very proud of that scene.

MENKEN: When we did [the first] preview…I'm sitting there going, “Wow! Look at this!” I look at David Geffen, and he said, “Yeah, wow, but wait a second—the cards, Alan!”

Those would be the reaction cards on which that era’s preview audiences would answer questions regarding how much they liked a film. Typically, producers were looking for 55% of a screening’s viewers to say they’d “recommend” the film. Little Shop’s first screening in San Jose got 13%. Oz asked Geffen to screen it again in LA to make sure this wasn’t an anomaly. The results were the same.

GEFFEN: People were hostile to the end of the film. They were hostile to the characters getting killed. We thought we were going to have a disaster.

OZ: The audience was against me because I killed people they loved, and it was a great lesson to learn. Onstage, they also die, but the actors come out for a bow. In movies, you don’t come out for a bow. You just die.

GREENE: [Onstage], my death is not as heartbreaking. It's a mixture. Just when you’re about to laugh, I’ll make you cry. Just when you’re about to cry, I’ll make you laugh.

GEFFEN: I think what the audience didn’t get was that this was a send-up of monster movies in the ’50s. They took it quite seriously. We made it so realistic that they were horrified by the end of the movie.

FERREN: The idea was, I want to go out smiling and happy. Now, I guess, it shows my personality. I went out smiling and happy, watching the world end.

OZ: They wouldn’t even release the movie if I didn’t change the ending…. The hardest of all was the terrible, terrible, terrible phone call I had to make after Richard Conway and his amazing crew made all those miniatures in that whole ending. I remember I had to call London from Los Angeles and say, “Richard, we’re not going to use any of it.”

What I also heard at the time [after the failed test screenings] was that there was a thought to try and get Rodney Dangerfield to do the voice of the plant, I assume to make it funny. My intent for the plant was to have it [be] a strong antagonist. If it was funny, there would have been no threat to Seymour or Audrey.

The team had to figure out a new finale that would stay true to the story and give Seymour and Audrey a happy ending. The solution? Seymour would electrocute the plant during their final showdown, and he and Audrey would finally get to move somewhere that’s green. But sitting outside of their dream home would be a small Audrey II, smiling at the camera.

OZ: The idea [came together] very fast. Howard and I knew exactly what had to happen. That part where the little plant smiles at the end was because I couldn’t make it a happy ending. It had to have some danger to it…. We went back [to London] for a month to reshoot.

Made on a budget of $25 million, including $5 million that wound up on the cutting-room floor, the film was unleashed on the public on December 19, 1986. It wound up doubling its budget at the box office, earning $54 million globally. A modest success, it didn’t necessarily set the world on fire—at least, not right away.

ARNOLD: Tisha and I had a really interesting moment. We decided to go see the movie in Times Square. We sat behind these two girls that were watching it, and we were like, “Okay, let’s go in when it’s dark so nobody recognizes us.”

CAMPBELL: There were these three girls sitting behind us. And [during the movie], they were like, “I’m so sick of these girls popping up out of nowhere!” [Laughs] So our first experience being able to watch our film, there were some haters behind us.

ARNOLD: Needless to say, I don’t watch myself anymore.

MENKEN: “Mean Green Mother” was nominated for the Academy Award, which was just amazing. I remember Levi Stubbs came out and sang “Mean Green Mother.” And I'm thinking, Wow! Well, I have a speech in my pocket. Who knows? Howard just goes, “Alan, you can relax. You’re not giving any speeches tonight.”

OZ: [When it came to home video], that’s when everything kind of exploded.

GREENE: [While currently touring with the movie], I get to see their love of Little Shop, their love of Audrey, even their love of me. I just hug everybody because I know they want it.

WEEKS: I went to see [Ellen on the tour recently]. It brought me to tears a couple of times…. They introduced me, and Ellen was surprised to see me. I was so happy to see her. We hugged and everything, and we talked a bit later on. But the warm reception that I got kind of brought me to tears because they were like, “Oh my gosh, it’s Ronette!” It just made me feel seen.

ARNOLD: I always said Little Shop of Horrors was a movie done before its time. But it stood the test of time and is still standing.

MENKEN: It is a true musical, and it’s driven by high-energy pop and rock, and it’s not about, “Oh, look how hip it is.”… It’s a thrill ride that really moves fast.

GEFFEN: I thought it was a terrific movie when we made it. I was very unhappy that we changed the ending…. I always wanted to restore it. And, as you know, we did. [In 2017 a version of the movie with the original ending played in theaters.]

OZ: I finally got to call Richard before he retired, saying, “Richard, finally they’re going to see your work.”

MORANIS: It’s become a point of discussion for people, whether they prefer one to the other, or if they’ve seen both of them. It’s prompted a couple of extra releases of different versions of the film.

OZ: I think [it resonates] because when you look at the movie, you know it’s not CGI…. It’s nice to show people what could be done when a lot of human beings get together and make something.

I think this would be as big a hit as the books.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm buzzing through the Dungeon Crawler Carl series this year, and my 8-year-old daughter gets so jealous every time she sees it. She loves cats, dinosaurs, and adventure, so in her mind, there's no reason she shouldn't be able to read it as well or watch the upcoming series when it premieres for those with a Peacock subscription.

Of course, anyone who has read the books knows that they're hardly appropriate for a young audience. One would have to remove all the gore, swearing, and raunchy jokes for it to even begin to pass for most parents, which gave me an idea. What if Princess Donut was able to retell the events of DCC, but in the way she'd tell it to her dinosaur "child," Mongo?

I love the way Princess Donut treats and refers to Mongo like he's a child, despite the fact that he's a raptor regularly tearing their enemies to bits. She's always worried about him being traumatized, or "appalled," which got me thinking. It would be hilarious to read Donut recalling their past adventures to Mongo, and self-censoring the raunch along the way.

I just imagine my daughter laughing as I'd tell her about Princess Donut dancing in the club, zapping goblins with her laser vision, and going on side tangents about her hatred for Cocker Spaniels. It would still be the Donut we know from the books, but she's adjusting it all for the audience it's intended for.

I think it would be important to have that, rather than standard narration. Donut is a gem of a character, and I think introducing children to that early on would only encourage them to check out the novels in full when they're of age later in life.

I've often thought about Carl being the narrator in Dungeon Crawler Carl, and how much the story might change if it were anyone else narrating. The things they'd focus on, compared to him, and the things they'd notice well before he did. I'm of the opinion that Donut might have a more entertaining telling of it all, which is part of the reason she's just the best.

Matt Dinniman Can Thank Jeopardy! For Making Dungeon Crawler Carl's Success Feel Real For His Mom's Friends

All this to say, part of this plight is because I also want to see how much I'd enjoy Donut retelling the story, even if it were geared toward children. Plus, there are already spinoffs in the works, like the upcoming comic featuring Florin.

If I could get the ball rolling on making Princess Donut's Bedtime Stories For Mongo, I definitely would. I'm not the author, however, so Matt Dinniman, if you have time between making the rest of the series, perhaps consider this pitch to sell the fun of Dungeon Crawler Carl to the children?

In the meantime, I'll keep reading the stories, waiting for the new books and announcements related to the upcoming series. I have a feeling we're about to be overwhelmed with news about the franchise over the next year, but I promise I won't let it break me.

#3671. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.
